paragraphs.text: Vertebral Column
Readings – Moore, pg. 439 – 482
Images – Netter, plates 19 – 23, 150 – 156
Overview
The “axis” (rotational element) of the axial skeleton
Composed of 33 vertebrae, 23 intervertebral disks
IV disks make up ¼ of length; changes through the day
Functions
Provides framework for axial skeleton
Allows us to stand upright
Movement
Individual movement between vertebrae is small, but collectively 23 joints can generate a massive amount of movement
Movement dependent on joint architecture
Regional differences (see Movements of the Vertebral Column)
Protection
Spinal cord rests in vertebral canal; protected from blunt trauma
Also protection for vena cava, aorta, trachea, esophagus; structures that would “kink” if not for proximity to vertebral column
Divided into 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 coccygeal vertebrae
Some variation exists in lumbar, sacral vertebral number
Inferior vertebrae larger than superior vertebrae
Due to increase in weight bearing further down column
Phenomenon reverses at sacrum; S1 largest, size decreases into coccyx; due to inferolateral diffusion of weight into lower limbs
General Structure of a “Typical” Vertebra
Body
Anterior segment of vertebrae
Cylindrical block shape
Regional differences in cross sectional shape
Regional differences in block height from anterior to posterior
Responsible for normal spinal curvatures (see spinal curvatures)
Main support for column
Each body accepts weight of superior vertebral bodies
Reason for increased size of lower vertebrae; greater base of support
Composed of
Outer shell of dense, compact bone
Rigid support
Inner core of spongy trabecular (cancellous) bone
Think: sponge toffee
Lightweight support
Trabeculae oriented in vertical/horizontal latticework
Osteoporosis – loss of bone mineral content, bone density
Selective loss in horizontal trabeculae results in decreased support, collapse of vertical trabeculae
Appears radiographically as vertical striations, with central column collapse due to central weakness (compact bone remains relatively strong)
Highly vascular; contains large quantities of hematopoietic red bone marrow
Different regions of ossification
Centrum – primary ossification center; inner core
Epiphysial ring – secondary ossification center located on circumference of superior/inferior surface
Arch
Posterior archway over vertebral foramen (location of spinal cord)
Responsible for spinal cord protection
Pedicles
“Feet” of the arch; anchors arch to body
Vertebral notches – concave superior/inferior surfaces of pedicles; form ½ of intervertebral foramen
Lamina
Broad, angled plates of bone
Bridge of the arch
Provides protection from posterior surface
Accepts anterior directed forces, dissipates away from vertebral foramen, towards pedicles
Laminectomy – surgical transection of the lamina; used to widen vertebral foramen, decompress spinal cord (see spinal stenosis)
Spinous process
Apex of the arch
Point of fusion of bilateral lamina
Protection, place for muscle attachment
Transverse processes
Project posterolaterally from interface of pedicles and lamina; articulation with ribs (thoracic vertebrae only) and site of muscle attachment
Superior and inferior articulating processes
Form the zygapophyseal joints between successive vertebrae
Articulating surfaces (facets) covered with articular cartilage
Pars interarticularis – column of bone between superior and inferior articulating processes
Ossification of Vertebrae
Most vertebral bone growth occurs in predictable fashion
Primary ossification centers start at 8 weeks of gestation with calcification of a cartilaginous model
Secondary ossification centers appear at puberty with continued growth at growth plates
Primary Ossification Centers
3 primary ossification centers within hyaline cartilage model
1 ossification center for body called centrum
2 bilateral ossification centers for neural arch
Arches fuse with body at neurocentral joints during 3rd year postpartum
NB: centrum of C1 fuses with centrum of C2, forming dens
Bilateral arches fuse at spinous process during 1st year postpartum

Spina bifida results from incomplete formation of hyaline cartilage leaving neural arch open posteriorly; asymptomatic spina bifida occulta common in general population (10-20%), often associated with tuft of hair on skin over site; more severe forms (e.g. spina bifida cystica) associated with neural damage, paralysis
Primordial costal elements appear bilateral to each vertebrae
Costal elements associated with thoracic vertebrae develop into ribs
Costal elements associated with cervical, lumbar vertebrae converge with transverse process

Cervical/lumbar ribs occasionally observed, creating confusion with surface inspection; cervical ribs can compress subclavicular structures, resulting in thoracic outlet syndrome (discussed further with upper limb)
Secondary Ossification Centers
5 secondary ossification centers
At tip of spinous process
At tip of each transverse process
Along superior and inferior rim of each vertebral body (annular epiphysis)
Annular epiphysis responsible for growth spurt during puberty
Produces slight biconcave appearance in typical vertebral body
Vertebral Morphology
Cervical Vertebrae
Vertebrae of the neck
Small rounded bodies
Complimentary concave superior surface, convex inferior surface along coronal plane
Uncinate process – lateral elevations along superior surface
Pedicles attach more lateral to body than in other vertebrae
Large vertebral foramen relative to vertebral body
Anterior and posterior tubercles on transverse processes
Sites for muscle attachment
“carotid” tubercles on C6
Site for manual compression of common carotid artery; control bleeding of distal lacerations to artery
Landmark for supraclavicular anesthesia injections
Foramen transversarium – canal within transverse processes
C1-C6 – passage of vertebral a. & v.
C7 – vertebral v. only
Spinous process short, often bifid
C7 – vertebral prominens – most prominent spinous process (visible superficially)
Atlas
C1 vertebrae
No body/spine; contains anterior/posterior arches/tubercles
Lateral masses
Support weight of skull
Transfers weight onto vertebral column inferiorly

Jefferson fracture – lateral masses wedge shaped (shorter medially); excessive axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water) forces lateral masses apart; can result in fracture to both anterior/posterior arches; damage to spinal cord uncommon (vertebral canal widens)
Superior articulating surface – articulates with occipital condyles (nodding)
Inferior articulating surface – for articulation with superior articulating surfaces on axis
Groove on posterior arch for vertebral artery
Axis
provides pivot joint for rotation of skull
Odontoid process (dens) – tooth-shaped structure; projects up posterior to anterior arch of atlas
Odontoid fractures
Superior articular surfaces – articulates with inferior articulating surfaces on atlas (gliding joint)

Hangman’s fracture – spondylolysis of C2 resulting from hyperextension of occiput; name comes from occurrence during executions, when noose’s knot is placed under chin; commonly associated with spinal cord injury
Thoracic Vertebrae
Heart shaped bodies
Deeper posterior
Long slender spinous processes, generally directed inferiorly
Tip of spinous process for each thoracic vertebra in line with body, IV foramen of inferior vertebrae; important to remember when landmarking through superficial palpation
Costal facets – sites for articulation with ribs
Facets for head of rib found on posterolateral surface of vertebral bodies
Articulating surface spans 2 vertebrae and IV disc
Inferior demifacet of superior vertebrae joins with superior demifacet of inferior vertebrae, considered one facet
Superior surface of T1 contains 1 full facet; complete articulation with head of 1st rib
Note that rib is numbered according to articulation with inferior vertebrae
Transverse facet – for articulation with tubercle of rib
Articulating facets oriented along coronal plane
Superior articulating surface faces posteriorly, inferior articulating surface faces anteriorly
T12 most commonly broken thoracic vertebrae; due to abrupt change in inferior architecture to accommodate 1st lumbar vertebrae
Lumbar Vertebrae
Large drum shape bodies
Deeper anteriorly (especially L5)
Transverse, wedge-shape spinous processes
Articulating facets oriented along sagittal/coronal plane
Superior articulating surfaces face medially, inferior articulating surfaces face laterally
Accessory process – located on base of transverse process; site of intertranversarii muscle insertion
Mammary process – located on superior articulating facet; insertion of multifidus
Variations in number of lumbar vertebrae
L5 sacralization – L5 partially/completely fuses with sacrum
S1 lumbarization – incomplete/total non-fusion of S1 with remainder of sacrum results in a mobile “L6” vertebrae
Both conditions may interfere with normal vertebral column biomechanics, resulting in pain and pathology over time
Sacral Vertebrae
5 fused vertebrae; no IV disks
Triangular shape – due to inferolateral dissipation of force through auricular surface to ileum
Think: keystone to archway
Auricular surface – roughened lateral surface for articulation with ileum of hip
Greatly limits shifting of lumbosacral joint
Pelvic surface smooth, concave, dorsal surface rough, convex
Forms bony posterior wall of pelvis
4 paired anterior/posterior sacral foramen – exit of ventral and dorsal roots, respectively
Promontory – anterior extension of sacrum at level of lumbosacral angle, supports vertebral column
Posterior sacral crests
Median crest – formed by fusion of spinous processes
Medial crests – formed by fusion of articular processes
Lateral crests – formed by fusion of transverse processes
Sacral hiatus – posterior opening of terminal portion of vertebral canal
Due to absence of (S4)S5 laminae, spinous processes
Landmarked using sacral cornue (extension of medial sacral crest)
Coccyx
Remnants of vestigial tail; composed of four small fused vertebrae
Site of muscle and ligament attachment
Coccygeal breaks common with falls; no effect on function, but activities that require pelvic muscle contraction very painful due to attachments/pulls on coccyx
General Characteristics of the Vertebral Column
Complimentary superior/inferior surfaces allow vertebrae to stack in predictable alignment
Think: LEGO blocks
Anterior column composed of vertebral bodies, IV discs
Bear majority of weight in erect position
Sudden loads, particularly in flexion (e.g. lifting heavy loads), or rapid hyperflexion (e.g. during head-on auto collisions) can result in compression fractures to vertebral bodies

With aging, outer collar of compact bone bears greater load, as central core compresses (increased biconcave appearance); can result in significant osteophyte (bone spur formation) in regions of excessive compressive forces, which can limit mobility, impinge surrounding structures
Vertebral foramen of individual vertebrae align to form continuous vertebral canal
Encases spinal cord, nerve roots
Superior/Inferior vertebral notches align to form intervertebral foramen; exit point for spinal nerves

Anterioinferior border of IV foramen made up of posterior surface of IV disc; degenerative changes to discs, posterior margins of vertebral bodies may encroach on vertebral notch; age related compression of vertebral bodies and clinical compression of discs following herniation may lead to loss of IV foramen height; any decrease in IV foramen size may compromise associated spinal nerve
Laminae stack to shield vertebral canal posteriorly, while providing mobility
Think: plate armour
Pars articularis form bilateral posterior columns
Accepts fraction of weight in erect position, especially in cervical, lumbar regions
Greater loads during extension, lateral flexion
Spondylolysis (vertebral break) – specific fractures of the pars interarticularis
Typically bilateral
Forceful extension of the neck (e.g. helmet tackle) can result in compression fractures within posterior columns
Results in anteroposterior instability in the vertebral column
Spondylolysthesis (vertebral slipping)
Anteroposterior instability (e.g. resulting from spondylolysis) may result in anterior displacement of superior vertebral body on inferior vertebral body
Most common between L5 and S1 vertebrae
Severity of symptoms dependent on degree of slippage, location of slip
Not to be confused with “slipped disc”
Ligaments
Vertebral column reinforced by numerous bands of ligaments
Anterior longitudinal ligament
Runs along the anterolateral aspect of the vertebral bodies
Only ligament to prevent hyperextension of the column
Whiplash injury – tearing of anterior longitudinal ligament and other soft tissue structures during hyper extension; may or may not include compression fractures
Posterior longitudinal ligament
Narrow band running along the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies
Weak resistance to hyperflexion
Reinforces the vertebral canal against posterior disc herniation; redirects herniations laterally toward IV foramen; implications for symptoms of disc herniation
Super/Interspinous ligaments
Continuous bands of connective tissue lying on top, in between spinous processes
Resist hyperflexion of column
In cervical region, supraspinous ligament deepens due to curvature of vertebrae, referred to as ligamentum nuchae
Intertransverse ligaments
Connect superior/inferior transverse processes
Resist excessive contralateral flexion
Ligamenta flava
Broad ligaments connecting superior/inferior lamina along posterior arch
Resist hyperflexion of column
Elastic properties – allows separation during flexion, remains taught in extension (avoids buckling, encroaching on vertebral canal)
Flava = yellow; unique color, due to high concentration of elastin protein
Spinal Curvatures
Not a perfectly linear structure; 4 normal curvatures exist
Cervical lordosis
Secondary curvature
Begins late in 3rd trimester, but most development occurs postnatally
Reformation of vertebral bodies as infant starts to lift head
Cervical vertebral bodies deeper anteriorly
Thoracic kyphosis
Primary curvature
Develops in womb
Height of thoracic vertebral body becomes greater posteriorly
Excessive kyphosis (“dowager’s hump”) seen in elderly, osteoporotic individuals; greater vertebral collapse anteriorly, due to increased load (anterior center of balance)
Lumbar lordosis
Secondary curvature
Develops postnatally; reformation of vertebral body as infant learns to crawl/walk
Excessive lumbar lordosis (“sway-back”) compensates for greater anterior loads (obesity, pregnancy); also results from weakened core musculature
Sacral kyphosis
Primary curvature
Develops in womb
Scoliosis – abnormal lateral curvature with rotation of the vertebrae; can be idiopathic (no known cause) or functional (e.g. resulting from leg length discrepancies)
Joints and Articulations
Joints of the Vertebral Bodies
Symphysis (fibrocartilagenous) joints that occur between adjacent vertebral bodies; differ from synovial joint (no space between bones)
Intervertebral disks – disks separate adjacent bones; provide shock absorption, resists excessive traction and allow for certain movements
Think: jelly donut
Nucleus pulposa – gelationous central core of intervertebral disk; semi-fluid ball-bearing
Nucleus pulposa dehydrates, hardens with age, resulting in loss of flexibility
Annulus fibrosus – concentric layers of oblique running fibers (adjacent layers run at 900 angles) provides tensile strength to resist expansion of nucleus pulposa
Thicker anteriorly than posteriorly

Disc herniation – sudden, excessive vertebral loading (especially during flexion) can rupture annulus fibrosus at weakest point, typically posterolaterally (think: slamming hand down on jelly donut); results in leaking of nucleus pulposa into vertebral foramen, compressing spinal cord, nerves
Zygapophyseal (facet) Joints
Joints of the posterior arch
Articulations between inferior articulating processes of superior vertebrae and superior articulating processes of inferior vertebrae
Connect segmental pars interarticularis, forming the posterior column
Synovial joints surrounded by joint capsule
Flat surfaces – gliding joints
Joint architecture changes along column; effect on movements allowed
Ankylosing spondylitis (stiffening spinal inflammation) – form of rheumatoid arthritis affecting the facet joints; over time, joints become rigid resulting in stiffening of the spine (“bamboo spine”)
Specialized Joints
Atlanto-occipital Joints
Synovial joints (condylar)
Allows for flexion extension (nodding); some sideways bending
Rotational motion limited due to contour of condyles, numerous atlanto-occipital ligaments
Anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane – fibrous bands joining anterior and posterior arches of atlas to base of skull
Tectoral membrane – continuation of posterior longitudinal ligament; connects atlas to inside of occiput
Atlanto-axial Joints
Lateral zygapophyseal joints
Planar orientation permits gliding between inferior articulating surface (atlas) and superior articulating surface (axis)
Medial joint
Synovial pivot joint between dens and anterior arch of atlas; allows for rotation of atlas on axis
Transverse ligament – holds dens in place; longitudinal bands combine to form cruciate ligament
Steele’s rule of thirds – for space between anterior, posterior arches, 1/3 occupied by dens, 1/3 occupied by spinal cord, 1/3 occupied by “space”
Rupture of transverse ligament typically results in anterior dislocation of C1 on C2; spinal cord compressed between dens and posterior arch, causing extensive damage
Alar ligaments – connect dens to occiput; limit range of motion for rotation of skull
Movements of the Vertebral Column
Results from plasticity of IV discs
Movements between individual vertebrae relatively small; summation of movement at 25 different segments produces large, complex, multiplanar movements of column
Combinations of flexion/extension, rotation, lateral flexion
Differences in joint architecture limit movements at different levels
Cervical region
Greater disc-to-body thickness results in greater movement
Zygapopyseal joints in transverse plane
Think: stacks of coins
All motions permitted

Dislocations more frequent in cervical region due to joint mobility; minor dislocations may self-correct (subluxate) without cord damage, due to wide canal; more serious dislocations (e.g. facet jumping) more likely to result in cord damage
Thoracic region
Low disc-to-body thickness limits motion
Zygapopyseal joints oriented in coronal plane
Bound together by strong ligaments, anchored to thoracic cage
Some lateral flexion, rotation, little to no flexion/extension
Lumbar region
Zygapopyseal joints oriented sagittally
Become more coronally oriented down column
Limits rotation in this region

paragraphs.text: Muscles of the Back
Readings – Moore, pg. 482 – 495
Images – Netter, plates 168 – 172
Overview
Refers to muscles originating off the vertebral column
Categorized as…
Extrinsic back muscles
Muscles insert on ribs, appendicular skeleton
Generate movements in upper appendages; no direct effects on movements of axial skeleton
Innervated by ventral rami of spinal nerves
Intrinsic back muscles
Muscles insert on axial skeleton
Direct effect on movements of the vertebral column
Innervated by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Extrinsic Back Muscles
Insert on ribs, appendicular skeleton
Generate movements in upper appendages; no direct effects on movements of axial skeleton
Mostly innervated by ventral rami of spinal nerves
Superficial Group
a.k.a posterior axioappendicular muscles
Act on shoulder girdle
move scapula, humerus relative to vertebral column
Trapezius
Origin
Superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7 - T12
Insertion
Lateral 1/3 of clavicle, acromion, and spine of scapula
Action
Elevates, retracts, depresses, and rotates scapula
Innervation
Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Notes
Attaches pectoral (shoulder) girdle to skull and vertebral column  -  assists in suspending upper limb
Dropped shoulder syndrome – weakness/paralysis of trapezius results in chronic depression of scapula; can lead to further strain on cervical vertebrae, cervical nerves
Superior, middle, and inferior fibers have different effects on scapula
Supplied by transverse cervical and dorsal scapular arteries
Latissimus dorsi
Origin
Spinous processes of T7 - T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inferior 3-4 ribs
Insertion
Floor of intertubercular groove of humerus
Action
Extends, adducts, and medially rotates humerus
Raises body toward arms during climbing
Innervation
Thoracodorsal nerve
Notes
Acts on shoulder joint
May attach to lower scapula
Upper part covered by trapezius
Supplied by thoracodorsal artery
Levator scapulae
Origin
Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C1 - C4
Insertion
Superior part of medial border of scapula (above spine)
Action
Elevates scapula; tilts glenoid cavity inferiorly by rotating scapula
Innervation
Dorsal scapular nerve; cervical nerves C3 and C4
Notes:
Lower part deep to trapezius
Supplied by dorsal scapular artery
Rhomboids (minor and major)  -  deep to trapezius
Origin
Minor:  nuchal ligament and spinous processes of C7 and T1
Major:  spinous processes of T2 - T5
Insertion
Medial border of scapula from spine to inferior angle
Action
Retract and rotate scapula; fix scapula to thoracic wall
Innervation
Dorsal scapular nerve
Notes:
Muscles not always clearly separated
Supplied by dorsal scapular artery
Deep Group
Thin serrated muscles
Insert on ribs
Most likely play a role in proprioception
Too small to assist with rib movement
Serratus posterior superior
Origin
Nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7 - T3
Insertion
Superior border of ribs 2-4 or 5
Action
Proprioception, elevates upper ribs
Innervation
Intercostal nerves 2-5
Serratus posterior inferior
Origin
Spinous processes of T11 - L2
Insertion
Inferior borders of ribs 8-12
Action
proprioception, depresses lower ribs
Innervation
Intercostal nerves 9-12
Intrinsic Back Muscles
Muscles insert on axial skeleton
Direct effect on movements of the vertebral column
Maintain posture
Movements of the trunk
Innervated by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Superficial Group
Splenius (capitis and cervicis)
Origin
Nuchal ligament and spinous processes of C7 – T3 or 4
Insertion
Splenius capitis - mastoid process and lateral 1/3 superior nuchal line
Splenius cervicis - transverse processes of C1 - C3 or 4
Action
Bilateral contraction – ipsilateral flexion, rotation of neck
Bilateral contraction – extension of neck
Innervation
Dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Notes
Splenius = bandage
Covers and holds deep neck muscles in position
Intermediate Group:
Erector spinae  (iliocostalis - lateral,  longissimus - intermediate,  spinalis - medial)
Enveloped by thoracolumbar fascia
Origin
Broad tendon from posterior iliac crest, posterior sacrum, sacral and inferior lumbar spinous processes, supraspinous ligament, ribs
Insertion
Iliocostalis (lumborum, thoracis, cervicis) - ribs and cervical transverse processes
Longissimus (thoracis, cervicis, capitis) - ribs, thoracic and cervical transverse processes, mastoid process of skull
Spinalis (thoracis, cervicis, capitis) – upper thoracic spinous processes, skull
Action
Acting bilaterally – extend vertebral column and head, maintain upright posture
Acting unilaterally – laterally bend vertebral column
Innervation
Dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Notes
Chief extensor of the vertebral column
Low back muscle strains
Erector spinae particularly susceptible to strain (muscle tears)
Acute strains – associated with sudden extension with excessive loads, often combined with trunk rotation
Education of proper lifting techniques, especially in susceptible populations (e.g. manual labor) important preventative medicine
Chronic strain – associated with habitual poor posture, especially excessive lumbar lordosis
Professional assessment of work stations in susceptible populations (e.g. office staff) can improve posture, avoid problems
Careful differential diagnosis necessary to rule out vertebral fractures/sprains
Deep Group:
Transversospinalis  muscles
Run from the tranverse process of inferior vertebrae to spinous process of superior vertebrae
(semispinalis - superficial,  multifidus - intermediate,  rotatores - deep)
Origin
Transverse processes of vertebrae
Insertion
Spinous processes of more superior vertebrae
Semispinalis (thoracis, cervicis, capitis) –  5-6 segments;
semispinalis capitis inserts on occipital bone
Multifidus - span 3-4 (2-4) segments
Rotatores - span 1-2 segments
Action
Bilateral – Head/vertebral extension
Unilateral – contralateral rotation
Important role in proprioceptive feedback
Innervation
Dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Notes
Semispinal capitis is usually pierced by greater occipital nerve
Multifidus is thick in lumbar region, semispinalis is thick in neck region
Minor muscles - proprioception
Interspinales – inbetween spinous processes
Intertransversarii – in between transverse processes
Levatores costarum – transverse processes to ribs
Nerves of the Back
Back primarily supplied by lower cervical and thoracic, lumbar nerves
Nerves exiting vertebral canal diverge to form ventral primary rami (larger anterior branch) and dorsal primary rami (smaller posterior branch)
Dorsal rami pierce intrinsic muscles of the back, providing their fibers with segmental motor innervation
Sensory branches continue past intrinsic muscles to skin of back
C4 - T6 – penetrate skin next to vertebral column
T7 - T12 – penetrate skin progressively more lateral (at fusion of latissimus dorsi with thoracolumbar fascia)
L1 – L3 – cluneal nerves emerge lateral to latissimus dorsi, supply skin over lower back, upper gluteal region
Superficial Anatomy
Back region contains minimal subcutaneous tissue
Allows identification of most superficial back muscles
Bilateral comparison can reveal imbalances
e.g. shoulders in baseball pitchers
May assist in diagnosis of joint problems
Identification of muscular wasting may assist in diagnosis of muscle paralysis, nerve lesions
Muscular borders create distinct anatomical landmarks
Many have clinical significance
Posterior median furrow
a.k.a. median longitudinal furrow, nuchal furrow
Thin region of skin between trapezius muscles, overlying the vertebral spinous processes
Continuous superiorly with nuchal groove overlying ligamentum nuchae
Continuous inferiorly with intergluteal cleft between buttocks
Allows identification, palpation of spinous processes
Diagnosis of scoliosis
Vertebral prominens
Spinous process of C7 vertebrae
Typically most prominent in back
Important landmark for counting vertebrae
Lumbar dimples
Found lateral to erector spinae prominence
Location of posterior superior iliac spine (on ileum)
Lines connecting dimples to intergluteal cleft and each form sacral triangle
Assists with landmarking of sacral hiatus
Common focal area for low back pain
Triangle of auscultation
Region defined by medial border of scapula, inferolateral border of trapezius, superior border of latissimus dorsi
Thin region of posterior thoracic wall (minimal muscle overlap)
Good site for stethoscope placement (identification of breath sounds)
Lumbar triangle
Region defined by inferolateral border of latissimus dorsi, iliac crest, posterior margin of external oblique
Infrequent site of herniation of abdominal structures (lumbar hernia)
Suboccipital Muscles
Small group of muscles at the base of the skull
Responsible for balance of skull on C1, movements of the occiput, C1, and C2 relative to one another
Large amount of proprioceptive feedback
Rectus capitis posterior major
Origin
Spinous process of C2
Insertion
Lateral inferior nuchal line
Action
Extension of skull
Innervation
Suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C1)
Rectus capitis posterior minor
Origin
Posterior arch (tubercle) of C1
Insertion
Medial inferior nuchal line
Action
Extension of skull
Innervation
Suboccipital nerve
Inferior oblique  (obliquus capitis inferior)  -  doesn’t attach to skull
Origin
Spinous process of C2
Insertion
Transverse process of C1
Action
Rotation of C1 on C2
Innervation
Suboccipital nerve
Superior oblique  (obliquus capitis superior)
Origin
Transverse process of C1
Insertion
Occipital bone between superior and inferior nuchal lines
Action
Extension of skull?
Innervation
Suboccipital nerve
Suboccipital muscle tension (typically stress related) common cause of head/neck pain
Suboccipital release – manual therapy technique to massage suboccipital muscles, relieve pain
The Suboccipital Triangle
Region defined by the borders of 3 suboccipital muscles
Rectus capitis posterior major
Inferior oblique
Superior oblique
Serves as reference point in finding important anatomical structures
Vertebral artery

Ascends to base of skull through transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae, takes sharp turn medially to pass horizontally along superior margin of posterior arch of atlas, curves again to run superiorly along spinal cord to enter foramen magnum of skull
Horizontal portion can be observed in suboccipital triangle, superior to posterior arch of atlas

Tortuous bony route increases risk of injury to vertebral artery; sudden, forceful movements may result in traumatic vertebral artery dissection (tearing of internal vessel lining); common form of stroke in younger people (35-45)
Suboccipital nerve
Stems from the dorsal ramus of C1 spinal nerve
Visible in suboccipital triangle
Supplies muscles of the suboccipital triangle
Greater occipital nerve
Stems from the doral ramus of C2 spinal nerve
Can be identified inferior to suboccipital triangle (inferior oblique muscle)
Pierces through semispinalis capitis muscle to provide sensory information to back of scalp
