paragraphs.text: Nerves, Spinal Cord, and Meninges
Readings – Netter Clinical Anatomy, pgs. 71 - 78
Overview
“Neural super‐highway”; relay center for afferent and efferent messages between CNS, PNS
Specific information travels collectively in tracts; like highway lanes
Afferent vs. efferent – North vs. South bound lanes
Afferent (sensory) more dorsal
Efferent (motor) more ventral
Information reaches destination through spinal nerves projecting off spinal cord; like off‐ramps to East/West bound streets
Segmental arrangement; neurons exit close to destination
Take exit ramp closest to destination
Reflected in dermatome map
Shingles
Cells of the Nervous System
Neurons – highly specialized cells that conduct electrical impulses throughout body
Fastest form of communication
Four principal components…
Signal reception at dendrites/receptors
Signal transport along axon
Myelinated axons – axons wrapped in layers of myelin from schwann cells (like a jelly role)
Provides insulation, improves conduction speed
Gives axon white appearance
Multiple Sclerosis – autoimmune attack against myelin sheaths; leads to inflammation, demyelination, and scarring
Unmyelinated
Signal transduction at axon terminus
Cell maintenance through organelles
3 Different classes, based on structure
Multipolar
Cell bodies found at one end of axon
Numerous dendrites attach directly to cell body
Structure of motoneurons (motor nerve cells)
Dendrites/body found in spinal cord, axon terminus in effector organs
Pseudounipolar
Cell bodies attach partway along axon through hillock
Structure of sensory neurons (sensory nerve cells)
Receptors found in effector organs, axon terminus in spinal cord
Bipolar
Cell bodies embedded partway along axon
Structure of sensory neurons for special senses
Neuroglia – support cells (e.g. schwann cells)
Help maintain neuronal function
Do not transmit electrical impulses
Divisions of the Nervous System
Central Nervous System (CNS) vs. Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
CNS – brain and spinal cord
PNS – spinal and cranial nerves
Somatic vs. Autonomic
Somatic nervous system
General sense perception from the periphery
Voluntary motor control of skeletal muscles
Autonomic nervous system
Visceral sensation from internal organs
Involuntary messages sent to effector organs (smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands)
Types of neurons
Afferent (sensory)
PNS to CNS
Sensory information brought to brain for processing
Efferent (Motor)
CNS to PNS
Signals to muscle tissue stimulate contraction
Interneurons
Found exclusively in CNS
Receive signals from/send signals to other neurons
Most abundant type of neuron (>90% of all neurons)
Spinal Cord
“Super”-super highway; relay center for afferent and efferent messages between the central and peripheral nervous systems
Makes up major volume of the vertebral canal
Tubular ellipsoid structure; approximately the shape, width of the pinky finger
Diameter not uniform along length
Cervical enlargement
~ C5 through T1 levels
Corresponds to location of brachial plexus – dense collection of nerves supplying upper appendages
Lumbosacral enlargement
~L1 through S1 levels of spinal
Supplies nerves to lumbar/sacral plexuses – neural traffic to lower appendices
Regions of enlargement particularly susceptible to symptomatic spinal stenosis (narrowing of the vertebral canal due to inflammation, structural collapse)
Starts at the inferior portion of the medulla oblongata (foramen magnum) and descends to the level of L1-L2

In embryos, the spinal cord and vertebral column are the same length; during fetal development, osteal tissue grows much faster than neural tissue; at birth the spinal cord only reaches level of L2-L3; continued growth of vertebral column increases this discrepancy
Terminal portion tapers to point called conus medullaris; protective coverings taper/fuse to form filum terminale; filum terminale passes through sacral hiatus, anchors spinal cord to coccyx
Lowest spinal nerves (below L2) continue inferiorly in bundle resembling horses tail (cauda equina) to exit through IV foramen
Spinal Cord in Cross Section
White matter (myelinated neural tissue) along cord’s periphery
Axons extending to/from PNS
Grey matter (non-myelinated neural tissue) makes up central core
Cell bodies and non-myelinated interneurons
Butterfly shape
Ventral horns – project anteriorly; cell bodies for lower motor neurons
Dorsal horns – project posteriorly
Lateral horns – present in lower thoracic, upper lumbar regions; cell bodies for autonomic nervous system
Cord incompletely divided by ventral median fissure anteriorly, dorsal median sulcus posteriorly
4 smaller sulci on posterior surface
Hollow central canal contains cerebrospinal fluid
Spinal Nerves
Spinal cord gives off 31 pairs of spinal nerves; names similar to vertebrae
8 cervical (C1 – C8)
12 thoracic (T1 – T12)
5 lumbar (C1 – C8)
5 sacral (S1 – S5)
1 coccygeal
Spinal cord injuries typically result in loss of function in all spinal nerves below lesion; extent of paralysis largely dictated by anatomic location of injury
Above C5 – breathing affected
C5-T1 – complete/incomplete quadriplegia
T1-L4 – paraplegia
L4-S1 – incomplete paraplegia
NB numbers above relate to spinal cord, not vertebral levels
Numbered according to level at which nerve exits vertebral canal
C1 emerges between occipital bone and C1
C1-7 exit above vertebrae of corresponding number
C8 exists between C7 and T1 vertebrae;
Remaining nerves exit below Vertebrae of corresponding number

Nerves exit through IV foramen; diseases that narrow IV foramen (disk herniation, compression fractures, arthritis, bone spurs) may impinge/irritate spinal nerves exiting foramen, resulting in referred pain; common at the level of L5 spinal nerve (relatively large nerve, relatively narrow IV foramen)
Spinal nerves – fusion of anterior ventral rootlets, posterior dorsal rootlets
Ventral rootlets
Efferent (motor) axons;
Impulses from CNS to PNS
Multipolar; cell bodies located in anterior horn
Dorsal rootlets
Afferent (sensory) neurons
PNS to CNS
Pseudounipolar; cell bodies located in mid-region of dorsal rootlet (dorsal root ganglia)
Past IV foramen, spinal nerves divide into anterior ventral, posterior dorsal rami (branches);
NB – anterior roots – motor, posterior roots – sensory; anterior/posterior rami – both sensory and motor
Nerves in Action – The Stretch reflex
Reflects the most simplistic type of neural relay
Process
Rapid stretch of muscle fibers triggers sensory receptor (muscle spindle)
Impulse travels along sensory nerve to spinal cord
Signal reaches axon terminus; stimulates…
Motoneuron in anterior horn
Signal travels along motoneuron axon back to muscle, triggers contraction
Interneuron in posterior horn
Interneuron has inhibitory effect on antagonistic muscle, preventing contraction
Message also travels to brain for interpretation
Dermatomes, Myotomes, and Peripheral Nerve Distribution
Importance in identifying/diagnosing neuropathies
Dermatome
Cutaneous segments supplied by single spinal cord segment
NB – some overlap between adjacent dermatomes
Myotome
Portion of skeletal muscle innervated by single spinal cord segment
Peripheral nerve distribution
Regions of skin/muscle supplied by a given peripheral nerve
Not always identical to dermatome/myotome
e.g. nerves fuse/split in brachial/lumbar/sacral plexus
Spinal Meninges
Central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) completely enveloped by 3 protective membranes (meninges)
Dura mater (hard mother)
Outer layer tough fibrous connective tissue
Forms loose sac around spinal cord
Projects out to each spinal nerve; tapers to contact nerves; fuse with epineurium (dural sleeves)
Tapers at sacral level, forming outer dural portion of filum terminale
Arachnoid mater (spider mother)
Middle layer
Thin, shiny sheath of elastic connective tissue on underside of dura mater
Dura/arachnoid mater form dural sac
Epidural space between sac and vertebrae; filled with adipose tissue, venous plexus
Epidural anesthesia – anasthetic injected in epidural space at level of lumbar vertebrae (typically L4/L5); diffuses and baths lower spinal nerves; ideal for lower limb surgeries, child birth
Caudal Anesthesia (epidural block); anasthetic injected in epidural space at level of sacrum
Subarachnoid space between sac and spinal cord
Contains cerebrospinal fluid; baths and nourishes spinal cord, prevents trauma
Arachnoid trabeculae – web-like extensions to spinal cord; stabilizes subarachnoid space
Space expands past conus medularis, forming lumbar cistern
Spinal anesthetic – anasthetic injected directly into subarachnoid space; quicker acting, cost effective; greater risks than with epidural, unable to catheterize; less common in developed countries

Lumbar puncture (spinal tap) – examination procedure, where CSF extracted from subarachnoid space; needle passes above/below L4 vertebral arch (past spinal cord; cauda equine pushed to side of needle); care need with young children (spinal cord lower)
Acute dehydration can decrease CSF volume, results in sagging, triggering pain receptors in dural sac; results in dural headache; common following alchol intoxication (i.e. hangover)
Pia mater (delicate mother)
Continuous with, inseparable from the spinal cord
Tapers at conus medularis, forming pial portion of filum terminale
Lateral tooth-like projections between IV foramen (denticulate ligaments); anchors spinal cord to dural sac
Region of vertebral column external to spinal cord called the epidural space; contains loose areolar connective tissue and part of vascular supply
Vascularization of the Spinal Cord
Blood supplied to spinal cord through numerous branches
Branches off vertebral, cervical arteries supply cervical region
Branches off posterior intercostal arteries supply thoracic region
Branches off lumbar, iliolumbar arteries supply terminal portion
Sacral arteries supply cauda equina
Give off dorsal and ventral radicular arterial branches, enter vertebral canal through IV foramen, run with dorsal and ventral rootlets, respectively
Certain branches (segmental medullary) anastamose with 3 separate longitudinal arteries (think: 3 elevators in skyscraper)
Single anterior spinal artery follows ventral median fissure
Gives off central branches along the length of the cord, which run posteriorly in the fissure towards the central canal
Paired posterior spinal arteries arise from the vertebral artery superiorly and run along the dorsal lateral sulci
Anterior and posterior spinal arteries anastamose with one another at the level of the conus medullaris

Spinal cord supplied by multiple spinal branches; anastomoses allow compensation if some spinal branches occluded (e.g. aortic surgical procedures); occlusion of certain major arteries [e.g. major segmental medullary artery (of Adamkiewicz)] can cause significant ischemia (compromised blood flow); results in weakness, paralysis
Blood drains into peripheral veins
3 anterior, 3 posterior longitudinal
Drainage continues into anterior/posterior venous plexuses in epidural space
from the epidural space; follow similar paths to radicular arteries out of the spinal cord
Cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space drains superiorly into the sulci of the brain

title: Nerves, Spinal Cord, and Meninges

paragraphs.text: The Shoulder
Images – Netter, plates 406-418
Overview
Junction between trunk and upper limb
Subdivided into…
Pectoral region – anterior
Deltoid region – lateral
Scapular region - posterior
Form fits function
Almost all movements of the upper limb involve positioning the hand for manual activities
Structure emphasizes range of motion
Stability is compromised, leading to wide variety of common injuries
Extensive musculature provides majority of support
Axioappendicular muscles – originate off the thorax to attach to scapula, clavicle, humerus
Scapulohumeral muscles – originate off the scapula to attach to the humerus
Pectoral Region
Anterior aspect of the shoulder
Overlaps with discussion of anterior thoracic wall (discussed in unit 3)
Composed of bone, muscle, fascial planes
Muscles collectively classified as anterior axioappendicular
Clavicle
Part of the pectoral girdle – bones that connect the axial and appendicular skeletons
Superior margin of pectoral region
Gives degree of protection to vital neurovascular structures beneath
“S” shaped bone that articulates with the sternum medially and anteriorly and with the scapula lateral and posteriorly

Structural weak point 2/3 along the mid-shaft of the clavicle; due to curvature, differences in ossification of regions (medial 2/3 endochondral, lateral 1/3 intramembranous); arguably the most commonly broken bone in the body; fracture causes prominent deformity, due to elevation of medial fragment due to muscle pull and sag of lateral aspect due to limb sag
Smooth superior surface; easily palpated through thin cutaneous tissue
Rough inferior surface due to muscle/ligament attachments
Triangular shaped sternal head articulates with manubrium, forming the sternoclavicular joint
Only direct articulation between axial and appendicular skeleton
Contains articular disc to assist with multiplanar motions
Joint reinforced, motion limited by strong ligaments
Acts as strut; subtle movements translate into larger movements of clavicular end, increasing shoulder range of motion
Think: boom arm of a crane
Broad, flat lateral end articulates with acromion process of scapula through acromioclavicular joint
Indirectly links scapula to axial skeleton
Minimal motions permitted, due to strong reinforcing ligaments

Shoulder separation – separation of the acromion process from the clavicle as a result of ligament tearing; not to be confused with shoulder dislocation; varying degrees, depending on severity; results in point tenderness; visible upon X-ray
Pectoralis Major Muscle
Most superficial portion of the pectoral region
Broad origin dividing the muscles into 2 heads
Sternal head – originates off the manubrium and body of sternum
Clavicular head – originates off the anteroinferior surface of the clavicle
Fibers converge to insert on the lateral ridge of the biciptal groove on the humerus
Adducts, horizontally flexes, medially rotates the shoulder
Innervated by medial/lateral pectoral nerves off the brachial plexus
Invested in pectoral fascia
Pectoralis Minor Muscle
Deeper part of pectoral region
Broad origin off ribs 3-5
Fibers converge upon coracoid process
Stabilizes scapula, elevates ribs
Innervated by medial pectoral nerve off the brachial plexus
Subclavius Muscle
Slender muscle connecting clavicle to the 1st rib
Anchors/depresses the clavicle during motion
Innervated by nerve to subclavius
Clavipectoral Fascia
Broad continuous sheet of fascia in the same plane as the pectoralis minor muscle
Divided into subregions, depending on location
Superior portion invests clavicle, subclavius muscle
Thickening of fascial sheet just inferior to subclavius runs from the coracoid process to the costochondral junction of the first rib; referred to as the costocoracoid ligament
Thins inferior to become costocoracoid membrane
Fascia continues inferiorly, enveloping pectoralis minor muscle
Single layer projects off lateral border of pectoralis minor to form suspensory ligament of the axilla
Pierced by neurovascular structures projecting to superficial pectoral region, upper limb
Scapular Region
Posterior aspect of the shoulder
Overlaps with discussion of the back (see Unit 1, lecture 2)
Primarily made up of bone and dense musculature
Muscles can be divided into
Posterior axioappendicular muscles – discussed previously with the back (see Unit 1, lecture 2)
Scapulohumeral (intrinsic shoulder) muscles
Scapula
Forms the bony wall of the posterior region of the shoulder
Triangular flat bone connecting clavicle to humerus
Only bony connection to axial skeleton is indirectly through acromioclavicular joint; mainly supported through numerous muscle attachments

Resting position, movement of scapula strong indicator of numerous muscle imbalances; assessments of shoulder pain should always include assessment of resting position, movement relative to humerus through multiplanar ROM (scapulohumeral rhythm)
3 borders (superior, medial, lateral) typically thicker than rest of body due to muscle pull
Head of scapula found at lateral angle
Site of glenoid fossa – articulates with humerus to form shoulder joint
Spine of scapula – prominent ridge on posterior aspect for muscle attachment
Divides posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae
Lateral end curves anteriorly, forming acromion process for articulation with clavicle at acromioclavicular joint
Acromion forms the roof of the subacromial tunnel; site of inflammation, pressure, supraspinatus tendinitis
Coracoid process projects off anterior surface – site of muscle attachment
The Rotator Cuff
Set of 4 intrinsic muscles that move the humerus relative to the scapula
NB: mnemonic SITS used to name muscles
Supraspinatus
Extensive origin off the supraspinous fossa
Fibers run in parallel fashion laterally; tendon passes through subacromial tunnel to insert on superior aspect of greater tubercle of humerus
Initiates abduction of shoulder, assists with fixation of humeral head
Innervated by suprascapular n.

Most common muscle affected in rotator cuff tears; likely due to angle of insertion onto humerus, passage through subacromial tunnel; tears can be due to acute trauma (e.g. falls) or chronic degeneration (e.g. severe tendinitis)
Infraspinatus
Extensive origin along the infraspinous fossa
Fibers converge to insert on middle aspect of greater tubercle
Shoulder fixator, external rotator
Innervated by suprascapular nerve
Teres Minor
Round muscle originating off inferior aspect of infraspinous fossa
Inserts on inferior aspect of greater tubercle
Often difficult to differentiate from infraspinatus muscle
Acts with infraspinatus to fixate, externally rotate shoulder
Innervated by axillary nerve
Subscapularis
Extensive origin off the subscapular fossa
Crosses anterior to the shoulder joint to insert on the lesser tubercle
Shoulder fixator, internal rotator
Innervated by upper/lower subscapular nerves
Teres Major
Rounded muscle similar in appearance to teres major
Originates just inferior to teres minor off the inferior angle of the scapula
Passes anterior to the shoulder joint to insert on the medial lip of the bicipital groove, just medial to the latissimus dorsi muscle
Medial rotator of shoulder
Innervated by lower subscapular nerve
NB: not part of rotator cuff (does not attach to tubercles)
Deltoid Region
Lateral aspect of the shoulder
Primarily consists of bone, muscle
Superior margin delineated by boney ridge formed by acromion process, lateral aspect of clavicle
Subacromial tunnel  - space immediately inferior to acromial ridge
Permits passage of supraspinatus tendon
Contains bursa to reduce friction during shoulder abduction

Bony frame prevents expansion of subacromial tunnel; inflammatory conditions (supraspinatus tendinitis, subacromial bursitis) results in increased pressure, pain in region; also results in greater wear on supraspinatus tendon, especially in full abducted position
Deltoid Muscle
Strong, thick muscle responsible for the rounded nature of the shoulder
Broad origin off the lateral rim of the acromion, clavicle
Fibers converge on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus
Convergence results in different motions, depending on fibers contracting
Anterior fibers flex shoulder
Posterior fibers extend shoulder
Intermediate fibers abduct at shoulder
Anterior/posterior fibers assist with abduction (stabilizers)

NB: deltoid unable to initiate abduction from anatomical position, due to 0 mechanical advantage (provides isometric resistance to gravitational sag in this position); supraspinatus, gravity required for first 150 of abduction
Innervated by axillary nerve off of brachial plexus

Axillary nerve closely associated with head, surgical neck of humerus; dislocations, breaks can result in acute nerve damage nerve, leading to deltoid paralysis; results in loss of ability to abduct shoulder past 150, flat shoulder deformity; chronic injury can also result from improper use of crutches, but is generally reversible
Glenohumeral Joint
The true shoulder joint
Articulation between the glenoid fossa of the scapula and the humeral head
Ball and socket joint – allows movements in all directions
Very shallow socket, compared to other ball and socket joints (e.g. hip)
Large range of motion with minimal stability; stability increased with isometric contraction of the rotator cuff muscles

Shoulder dislocations common due to instability of joint; humeral head typically dislocates anterior and inferior; posterior/superior dislocation less common, due to support offered by scapular spine, acromion; head commonly visible as bulge in armpit when arm is abducted
Muscular Boundaries and Spaces
Shoulder encases the axilla
Space intermediate to thorax and upper appendage, mostly inferior to the shoulder joint
Represents throughway for numerous structures passing from thorax to the upper limb
Sub-branches supply shoulder region
Think: off-ramps from the highway
Distinct spaces exist defined by muscular boundaries
Permit the passage of these sub-branches (discussed later) to their destinations
Triangular Space
a.k.a medial axillary space, superior triangular space
Superior border – Teres minor (subscapularis)
Inferior border – Teres Major
Lateral border – Long head of triceps brachii
Quadrangular Space
a.k.a lateral axillary space
Medial border – Long head of triceps brachii
Lateral border – surgical neck of humerus
Superior border – Teres minor (subscapularis)
Inferior border – Teres major
Triangular Interval
a.k.a inferior triangular space
Superior border – Teres major
Medial border – long head of triceps brachii
Lateral border – lateral head of triceps brachii
The Breast
The mammary gland is composed of glandular tissue embedded in adipose tissue, suspended by ligaments, and containing small arteries, nerves and lymphatics
Glands exist in pockets (lobules)
Milk produced in lobules drains into lactiferous ductules that collect into lactiferous ducts
Approximately 4 – 18 terminal ducts drain into the nipple
Lactiferous sinus just proximal to termination of duct; expresses milk in lactating woman with suckling, manual compression
Suspensory ligaments of the breast (Cooper’s ligaments) provide support the breast tissue, anchoring the breast to the dermis
With time, ligaments develop laxity, resulting in sagging breasts with advanced age
Separated from the pectoralis major by the retromammilary space
Divided into quadrants for localization of tumors/cysts
Superior lateral
Contains a superior extension known as the axillary process
Superior medial
Inferior lateral
Inferior medial
Breast cancer
Carcinoma of the breast – typically adenocarcinomas arising from the epithelial tissue surrounding the lactiferous ducts
Can result in hard masses within the mammary tissue, itself, noticeable upon palpation
Once metastasized, cancerous cells can pass into the lymphatic system
Disruptions in lymphatic drainage may lead to irregularities in breast tissue, noticeable upon visible inspection
The Axilla
Readings – Moore, pgs. 713-726
Images – Netter, plates 407-418
Overview
Pyramidal region found deep to the shoulder region
“Gateway” for many structures passing from the neck to the upper limb
Boundaries of the Axilla
Superior
Location of the apex of the pyramid
Bony boundary formed by clavicle, 1st rib, and scapula
Passage for structures passing between neck and axilla
Anterior
Wall formed by the pectoral region of the shoulder
Border ends inferiorly at the anterior axillary fold
Formed by the lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle
Posterior
Wall formed by the body of the scapula, associated scapulohumeral muscles, and latissimus dorsi muscle
Border ends inferiorly with the posterior axillary fold
Composed of both latissimus doris, teres major muscles
Medial
Formed by lateral border of rib cage and overlying musculature
Serratus Anterior Muscle
Most superficial portion of the medial wall of the axilla
Broad origin off of ribs 1 through 8
Named for serrated appearance of muscle origin
Wraps posteriorly to insert on the medial border of the scapula
Contracts to protract the scapula (pull arm forward)
Important muscle in quadrupeds to elevate thorax while walking
Innervated by long thoracic nerve

Long thoracic nerve can be injured during axillary surgeries, trauma (object gets jammed in axilla), resulting in paralysis of serratus anterior; results in scapular winging in push-up position (unable to hold scapula against body wall)
Lateral
Small boundary between the insertions of pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi
Humerus
Bone of the brachium (arm)
Long bone that articulates with scapula proximally, radius/ulna distally
Head articulates with glenoid fossa of scapula
Anatomical neck – remnant of the epiphyseal plate
Surgical neck – common site for fractures; clinical importance
Surgical neck is a common site for humeral fractures, due to its small diameter; danger is related to numerous neurovascular structures that lie in close approximation to this region
Shaft extends to elbow joint
Greater and lesser tubercles – sites for attachement of the rotator cuff muscles
Intertubercular groove – divot in humeral shaft between tubercles; location of the biceps brachii tendon
Radial (spiral groove) – runs lateral and inferior along posterior shaft; impression made by radial nerve
Deltoid tuberosity – attachment point for deltoid muscle
Distal region articulates with both radius and ulna, forming the elbow joint
Trochlea – pulley shaped segment that articulates with the ulna
Capitulum – small head shape segment that articulates with the radius
Olecranon fossa – accommodates the olecranon during extension
Coronoid fossa – accommodates the coronoid process during flexion
Medial and lateral epicondyles – sites for muscular attachment
Floor
Marked by the axillary fascia and overlying skin
Axillary fascial is continuous with pectoral fascia, suspensory ligament of the axilla anteriorly and with the fascia surrounding the latissimus dorsi posteriorly
Contents of the Axilla
Axillary Artery
Continuation of the subclavian artery as it passes the first rib to enter the axilla
Divided into 3 regions according to proximity to pectoralis minor muscle
1st segment proximal to pectoralis minor, 2nd segment posterior to pec minor, 3rd segment distal to pec minor
Each region gives off corresponding number of branches (1st gives of 1, 2nd gives off 2, 3rd gives off 3)
Region 1
Superior thoracic artery – supplies the superior part of the pectoral region (subclavius, intercostal spaces 1 and 2, portions of pectoralis major/minor, serratus anterior
Common site for aneurism (pathological bulging of vascular wall); may compress closely associated nerves of the brachial plexus, resulting in pain, parasthesia
Region 2
Thoracoacromial trunk – gives rise to 4 distinct branches
Clavicular – runs medially to sternoclavicular joint
Pectoral – runs anteriorly between the pectoralis major and minor muscles, providing the majority of their blood supply
Acromial – runs laterally, passing superior to the coracoid process to the acromioclavicular joint
Deltoid – runs laterally and through the deltopectoral groove, supplying pectoralis major and deltoid muscles

Lateral thoracic artery – descends lateral to the pectoralis minor muscle and along the lateral surface of the thoracic cage; supplies serratus anterior, intercostal muscles, and the lateral part of the pectoralis major muscle
Region 3
Subscapular artery – relatively large artery supplying 2 distinct branches
Circumflex scapular artery – passes through triangular space to supply structures of the infraspinous fossa
Anterior humeral circumflex artery – passes anterior to the humerus, deep to the anterior compartment muscles
Posterior humeral circumflex artery – passes through the quadrangular space to supply the back of the shoulder
Numerous anastomoses exist between the branches of the axillary artery and with other arteries; can result in rerouting of blood through collateral circulation during axillary artery compression
Axillary Vein
Accompanies axillary artery, most often lying anteromedial to it
Numerous branches that typically (though not always) accompany the arteries
Great deal of variability in position, number of branches
Brachial Plexus
Neural bundles that emerge from the lower cervical, upper thoracic spinal nerves to supply the shoulder and upper appendage
Converge, diverge in predictable fashion as they course through the neck and axilla (although variations exist)
Divided into 5 regions based on sites of convergence/divergence
Each region gives off distinct nerve branches
Roots
Term given to the ventral rami of C5 through T1 that emerge between the medial and lateral scalene muscles (described in head and neck)
Prefixed brachial plexus – C4-C8
Postfixed brachial plexus – C6-T2
Represent the most proximal portion of the brachial plexus
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5)
Branch of C5 that runs posteriorly between the scapula and vertebral column
Supplies rhomboid muscles
Long thoracic nerve
Fusion of branches from C5, C6, C7
Travels along thoracic cage to supply serratus anterior

Erb-Duchenne palsy – tearing of the upper roots (typically C5, C6) due to traction; results from forceful contralateral flexion of neck (falling on side of head, shoulder, pulling of child’s head during delivery); loss of scapular retraction, elbow flexors results in characteristic medial rotation of shoulder, extension at elbow (“waiter’s tip” sign)

Klumpke’s palsy – tearing of the lower roots (typically C8, T1) due to traction; results from forceful abduction, pulling on arm (grasping object to break fall, pulling of child’s arm during delivery); most serious affect is on intrinsic hand muscles, resulting in true claw hand (see notes on The Hand for further explanation)
Trunks
Located in the neck, superior to the clavicle
3 separate trunks identified
Superior trunk – formed from convergence of C5, C6
Middle trunk – the continuation of C7 ventral rami
Inferior trunk – formed from the convergence of C8, T1
Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
Branches from the superior trunk
Runs laterally with the suprascapular artery to the supraspinous fossa, continues along to the infraspinous fossa
NB: nerve passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament in the scapular notch, artery passes over ligament (think: army over navy)
Nerve to subclavius (C5, C6)
Small branch off the superior trunk that supplies the subclavius muscle
Chronic compression/traction of superior trunk can occur with excessive loads (e.g. heavy backpack); affects elbow flexors, extensors
Divisions
Short region found deep to the clavicle
Denotes splitting of all 3 trunks into anterior, posterior segments
Cords
Found distal to the clavicle in close approximation to the axillary artery
Site of characteristic convergence of the divisions
Named for proximity to axillary artery
Lateral cord – formed by the fusion of the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks
Medial cord – continuation of the anterior division of the lower trunk
Posterior cord – formed by the fusion of the 3 posterior divisions
Medial (C8, T1) and lateral (C5, C6, C7)pectoral nerves
Branches named according to their respective cords
NB: in thorax, lateral pectoral nerve appears medial
Medial branch supplies pectoralis minor, continues on to supply pectoralis major; lateral branch bypasses pectoralis minor to exclusively supply pectoralis major
Medial Brachial/Antebrachial nerves (C8, T1)
Branches off the medial cord
Continue through the medial aspect of the arm/forearm to provide cutaneous innervation to these regions
Upper (C5) and lower (C6) subscapular nerves
Branches off the posterior cord
Project posteriorly to subscapular fossa to supply subscapularis; lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major
Thoracodorsal nerve (C6-8)
Branches off the posterior cord (between upper and lower subscapular nerve)
Runs posteriorly along thoracic wall to supply latissimus dorsi
Terminal branches
Last portion of the brachial plexus
Collection of nerves that continue into the upper limb
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-7)
Continuation of lateral cord
Supplies motor innervation to the anterior compartment of the arm
Cutaneous branch continues as lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Ulnar Nerve (C8-T1)
Continuation of the medial cord
Supplies muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm, hand
Median Nerve (C6-T1)
Receives branches from both medial, lateral cords
Supplies muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm, hand
Axillary Nerve (C5-6)
One of two branches off the posterior cord
Runs through quadrangular space with posterior humeral circumflex artery
Innervates deltoid, teres minor muscle
Radial Nerve (C5-T1)
Larger branch of posterior cord
Supplies all muscles of the posterior compartments of the arm, forearm

Prolonged superiorly directed pressure on axilla may result in radial (and axillary) neuropathy, affecting all arm/forearm extensors; can result from improperly fitted crutch or falling asleep across a chair (“Saturday night palsy”)
Lymphatics
5 groups of lymph nodes situated through axilla
Organization reflects pyramidal shape of the axilla
Pectoral nodes
Found along medial wall of axilla
Receive lymph from anterior wall, breast tissue
Metastasized breast cancer cells may pass from the subaerolear lymphatic plexus to the pectoral lymph nodes in the axilla
If cells become lodges in nodes, they continue to replicate, resulting in enlargement of the nodes detectable upon palpation
Cells may advance to the central, axial nodes resulting in further enlargments
Biopsy of lymphatic tissue important in ascertaining spread of carcinoma in the breast
Subscapular nodes
Found posteriorly in the inferior portion of the axilla
Receive lymph from posterior thoracic wall
Humeral (lateral) nodes
Found laterally in the inferior portion of the axilla
Drain most lymph from the upper arm
Central nodes
Found deep to the pectoralis minor
Drain lymph from the 3 inferior groups
Apical nodes
Found at the apex of the axilla
Drain the central nodes and other regions in the area
Ultimately drains into subclavian nodes and back into venous circulation

Any infection of the upper limb, shoulder region may result in lymphangitis (inflammation of the lymphatics); resulting in swelling, tenderness; may be mistaken by lay person as an indication of breast cancer
The Brachium
Readings – Netter’s Clinical Anatomy, pgs. 362 – 366
Overview
a.k.a. the arm
Region of upper limb between shoulder and elbow
Contains the humerus
Divided into anterior, posterior compartments
Compartments divided by medial and lateral muscular septa – bands of connective tissue thicker than typical epimysium
Both septa provide transit for vessels, nerves travelling between axilla and antebrachium
Neurovascular compartment
Found within the medial aspect of the brachium
Made up of large collection of vessels, nerves embedded in loose areolar, adipose tissue
Location provides protection to structures from humerus
Anterior Compartment
Muscular compartment anterior to the humerus
Muscles responsible for flexion of shoulder, elbow joints
All muscles receive innervation from musculocutaneous nerve
Coracobrachialis
Fusiform muscle running from coracoid process to medial shaft of humerus
Flexes, adducts shoulder
Stabilizes shoulder joint by resisting inferior displacement of humerus (gravity, carried load)
Biceps Brachii
Fusiform muscle
2 heads converge on a single insertion point
Long head runs through intertubercular groove, curves medially at shoulder joint to attach to supraglenoid tubercle of scapula
Tendon surrounded by synovial sheath to reduce friction in intertubercular groove

Ruptured biceps tendon – tearing of tendon of long head of biceps muscle due to excessive wear; unopposed muscle bunches up in anterior compartment, resulting in “Popeye’s deformity”; minimal loss of function, due to continued action of short head; surgically repaired in young and athletic individuals, involving attaching the long head to the proximal shaft of the humerus
Short head has more direct origin from coracoid process
Thick round tendon inserts on radial tuberosity
Bicipital aponeurosis – broad, flat portion of tendon that curves medially
Continuous with antebrachial fascia
Provides protection for deep neurovascular structures
3 joint muscle
Flexion of shoulder joint
Flexion of elbow joint
Strong supinator of superior radioulnar joint
Brachialis
Fusiform muscle originating from anterior shaft of humerus
Broad muscle crossing anterior to elbow joint to insert on proximal portion of anterior ulna
Principle flexor of elbow; strong flexor at all joint angles
Posterior Compartment
Muscular compartment  posterior to humerus
Muscles responsible for extension of shoulder, elbow
Innervated by radial nerve
Triceps Brachii
Fusiform muscle composed of 3 heads converging on a single insertion point
Long head originates off infraglenoid tubercle
2 joint muscle – extension of shoulder, elbow
Stabilizes shoulder joint by resisting inferior displacement of humerus (gravity, carried load)
Lateral head originates off proximal posterior shaft of humerus
Strongest extensor of elbow
Medial head originates off distal posterior shaft of humerus; proximal portion lies deep to long head
Most active extensor of elbow
Anconeus
Runs medially from lateral epicondyle to olecranon
Accessory extensor
Tenses joint capsule to prevent pinching
Cubital Fossa
Depression on the anterior aspect of the elbow
Filled with variable amounts of fat and neurovascular structures
Triangular space with 3 boundaries
Imaginary line connecting epicondyles
Lateral border of pronator teres
Medial border of brachioradialis
Median cubital vein
Interconnection between the basilic and cephalic veins found within the subcutaneous tissue overlying the cubital fossa
Common site for blood draws, due to superficial location, ease of access
Brachial Artery
Principle artery of the brachium
Continuation of axillary artery past inferior border of teres major
Runs in large neurovascular compartment with veins, nerves, lymphatics
Starts medially, crosses anterior to coracobrachialis, travels posterior to medial border of biceps brachii to reach cubital fossa
Terminates at cubital fossa, where it splits into radial, ulnar arteries
Gives off numerous branches
Includes unnamed muscular branches
Several branches anastomose (merge with) inferior branches in the forearm
Forms collateral circulation
Think: collector lanes
Allow rerouting of blood when brachial artery compressed (e.g. in elbow flexion)
Profunda Brachii (Deep Artery of the Arm)
Branches off the brachial artery just past teres major
Runs with radial nerve through spiral groove in posterior compartment
Vascular supply for posterior compartment of the arm
Divides at variable level along shaft
Radial collateral branch runs anterior to epicondyle
Anastomosis with recurrent radial artery
Middle collateral branch runs posterior to epicondyle
Anastomosis with recurrent interosseus artery
Humeral Nutrient Artery
Small branch just distal to coracobrachialis
Penetrates nutrient foramen of humerus to supply bone tissue
Superior Ulnar Collateral Artery
Branches mid-brachium to run with the ulnar nerve
Runs posterior to medial epicondyle
Anastomoses with posterior ulnar recurrent artery
Inferior Ulnar Collateral Artery
Branches just proximal to the medial epicondyle
Crosses the elbow joint anterior to medial epicondyle
Anastomoses with anterior ulnar recurrent artery
Veins of the Brachium
More numerous, complex than arteries
Generally follow same path, given same names as accompanying arteries
Brachial Vein
Accompanies brachial artery to drain blood into axillary vein
Observed as venae comitantes – 2 paired vessels on either side of the artery
Arrangement common in the appendages
Commonly exist with complex branching
Basilic Vein
Subcutaneous vessel on the medial aspect of the arm
Dives through the fascia of the brachium to fuse with the brachial vein, forming the axillary vein
Cephalic Vein
Subcutaneous vessel on the lateral aspect of the arm
Runs superiorly in the deltopectoral groove
Pierces the clavipectoral fascia to drain in the axillary vein
Nerves of the Brachium
Four terminal branches off the brachial plexus pass through the arm
Only 2 innervate brachial structures
Additional cutaneous branches also pass through the brachium
Musculocutaneous nerve
Terminal branch off the brachial plexus
Pierces the coracobrachialis to enter the anterior compartment
Provides innervation to biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis
Radial Nerve
Terminal branch off the brachial plexus
Can be viewed in the triangular interval between long and lateral heads of triceps brachii
Travels along spiral groove, piercing lateral muscular septum to emerges anterior to lateral epicondyle and continue into forearm
Gives extensive branches to triceps brachii in the posterior compartment
Provides numerous cutaneous branches to the skin along the back of the arm
Median Nerve
Travels in neurovascular compartment with brachial artery/vein
Passes with brachial artery in the middle of the cubital fossa
No direct innervation in the brachium, continues to antebrachium to innervate anterior compartment, hand
Ulnar Nerve
Travels in neurovascular compartment posterior to brachial artery/vein, median nerve
Passes posterior to medial epicondyle to enter antebrachium
Sits in wedge shaped depression between epicondyle and olecranon; perturbation results in transient parasthesia, resulting in “pins and needles”; commonly referred to as the “funny bone”
No direct innervation in the brachium, continues to antebrachium to innervate anterior compartment, hand
The Antebrachium
Readings – Netter’s Clinical Anatomy, pgs. 366 - 377
Overview
a.k.a. the forearm
Extends from the elbow to the wrist
Consists of 2 bones joined by interosseus membrane (long, tough connective tissue)
Loose arrangement permits pronation/supination of the forearm (effectively “rotation” of wrist)
NB: wrist, itself, is an ellipsoid joint, which doesn’t permit rotation
Arrangement divides forearm into anterior/Posterior
Muscular compartments acting upon wrist/digits
Muscle bellies located in proximal forearm with long tendons extending to hand
For many muscles, proximal attachment point extends past elbow joint
Decreases bulk of distal forearm/hand to maximize function
Can lead to clinical problems (e.g. tendinitis)
Bones of the Antebrachium
Ulna
Lies on the medial aspect of the forearm
Much larger proximally, tapering at the wrist
Trochlear notch - deep concave surface for articulation with trochlea of humerus at elbow
Olecranon process projects posteriorly
Coronoid process projects anteriorly
Radial notch lies inferior to trochlear notch for articulation with head of radius
Shaft terminates in ulnar head for articulation at the wrist joint
Styloid process increases concavity of wrist joint
Radius
Lies on the lateral aspect of the forearm
Much larger distally, making up most of the proximal surface of the wrist joint
Smooth round radial head articulates with ulna in the radial notch
Rotates in spot, producing pronation/supination
Held in place with annular ligament
Distal dorsal surface has numerous grooves which accommodate tendons of the posterior compartment of the antebrachium
Styloid process increases concavity, surface area contact of wrist joint
Anterior Compartment
In anatomical position, located anterior to radius/ulna/interosseus membrane
Made up of muscles (mostly proximal) and tendons (distal) that flex the wrist/digits, pronate the forearm
Almost entirely innervated by median nerve
2 muscles receive innervation from ulnar nerve
Muscles crossing the wrist joint held in place by flexor retinaculum – prevents bowstringing of tendons during flexion
Digital flexors separated from wrist flexors by transverse carpal ligament – pass through deeper region known as carpal tunnel
Most long tendons covered in synovial sheath
Long synovial membrane that serves to reduce friction between tendon and surroundings
Think: Slipper snake toy
Divided into 3 principle layers, according to depth
Superficial Muscle Layer
Primarily originate off the common flexor tendon attached to the medial epicondyle/supracondylar ridge
Golfer’s elbow – term to describe medial epicondylitis; much less common that lateral epicondylitis
Flexor Carpi Ulnaris
Most medial of the superficial compartment
In addition to common flexor tendon origin (humeral head), also wraps posteriorly to attach to olecranon (ulnar head)
Ulnar nerve enters forearm between these origin points
Broad attachment to pisiform, hook of hamate, and proximal portion of 5th metacarpal
Only anterior compartment muscle to be fully innervated by ulnar nerve
Produces wrist flexion, ulnar deviation
Palmaris Longus
Found lateral to the flexor carpi ulnaris
Vestigial muscle – absent in ~14% of the population
Inserts onto flexor retinaculum, palmar aponeurosis
Tenses palmar aponeurosis
Flexor Carpi Radialis
Radial counterpart to flexor carpi ulnaris
Inserts on base of second metacarpal
Produces wrist flexion, radial deviation
Pronator Teres
Most lateral of the superficial compartment
In addition to common flexor tendon origin (humeral head), second attachment to coronoid process (ulnar head)
Median nerve passes between these muscles
Round muscle that runs obliquely to insert on lateral surface of radius
Pronator of the forearm
Intermediate Muscle Layer
Originates off medial epicondyle, anterior surface of antebrachium
Consists of single muscle
Flexor Digitorum Superficialis
Extensive origin
Humeroulnar head – originates off common flexor tendon, coronoid process deep to pronator teres
Radial head – originates off proximal portion of radius
Muscle splits to produce 4 tendons that run distally towards wrist
Tendons pass through superficial part of carpal tunnel
Stacked in 2x2 formation to pass through narrow part of tunnel
Tendons insert past proximal interphalangeal joint of digits 2 through 5
Work independently to flex all joints up to proximal interphalangeal joints
Does not act upon distal interphalangeal joints or proximal interphalangeal joint of digit 1 (see “The hand” for details)
Deep Muscle Layer
Originates off the anterior surface of the antebrachium
Does not cross elbow joint
Flexor Digitorum Profundus
Broad origin off the anterior surface of the ulna, medial half of the interosseus ligament
Muscle splits to produce 4 tendons that run distally towards wrist
Tendons pass through deep part of carpal tunnel
Run side-by-side through wide part of tunnel
Inserts on the distal phalanges of digits 2 through 5
Receives innervation from ulnar nerve
Medial (ulnar) half innervated by ulnar nerve, lateral (radial) half innervated by median nerve
Flexes all hinge joints of the wrist, hand
No effect on digit 1
Flexor Pollicis Longus
Broad origin off the anterior surface of the radius, lateral half of the interosseus ligament
Tendon runs through lateral aspect of carpal tunnel to insert on distal phalanx of 1st digit
Contributes to flexion of wrist, all joints of 1st phalanx
Pronator Quadratus
Most distal origin of all antebrachium muscles
Square shaped muscle originating off distal anterior surface of ulna to insert on distal anterior surface of radius
Principle pronator of the forearm
Posterior Compartment
In anatomical position, located posterior to radius/ulna/interosseus membrane
Muscles principally involved in extension of wrist/digits, supination
Some important exceptions
Tendons crossing wrist held in place by extensor retinaculum
6 distinct compartments
All muscles innervated by muscular branches of radial nerve
Divided into 3 separate groups
Superficial Muscle Layer
Primarily originate off the lateral epicondyle and supracondylar ridge of the humerus

Tennis elbow – term to describe lateral epicondylitis; results from inflammation to the periosteum over the lateral epicondyle due to repetitive forceful extension, typically against load (e.g. repetitive backhands in racket sports)
Brachioradialis
Originates off the supracondylar ridge
Projects over the lateral border of the radius to insert on its anterior surface
Unique among posterior compartment muscles in that is crosses anterior to the elbow to flex this joint
Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus
Originates off the supracondylar ridge inferior to brachioradialis
Tendon runs under outcropping muscles to pass into wrist
Inserts posteriorly on the base of the 2nd metacarpal
Produces wrist extension, radial deviation
Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
Originates as part of the common extensor group off the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Tendon runs under outcropping muscles to pass into wrist
Inserts posteriorly on the base of the 3rd metacarpal
Produces wrist extension, radial deviation
Extensor digitorum
Originates as part of the common extensor group off the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Muscle splits to produce 4 tendons that pass over outcropping muscles to cross wrist
Tendons continue to distal phalanges of digits 2 through 5 through extensor hood (see notes on “The Hand”)
Produces extension of digits 2 through 5
Linking of tendons through oblique intertendinous connections forces digits to function as a group
Extensor Digiti Minimi
Small fusiform muscle blended into extensor digitorum muscle
Tendon passes wrist joint through separate compartment in retinaculum than extensor digitorum
Inserts on the extensor hood of the 5th metacarpal bone
Contributes to extension of the 5th digit
Extensor Carpi Ulnaris
Originates as part of the common extensor group off the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Tendon runs within groove between ulnar head and styloid process to reach wrist
Muscle passes under retinaculum to insert on the base on the 5th metacarpal
Produces wrist extension, ulnar deviation
Deep Layer
Muscles originate of the posterior surface of the radius/ulna/
Supinator
Originates off the posterior surface of the ulna
Runs lateral and inferior to insert on the lateral surface of the radius
Muscle “corkscrews” during pronation, winding around the radius
Muscle contracts to supinate the forearm
Extensor Indices
Originates off the distal 2/3rds of the radius, interosseus membrane
Tendon runs under the extensor retinaculum inferior to extensor digitorum muscle to insert on the extensor expansion of the 2nd digit
Contracts to generate isolated extension of the second digit
Outcropping Muscles
Subset of the Deep Muscles
Tendons run obliquely to reach the thumb
Extensor Pollicis Longus
Originates off the ulna, interosseus membrane proximal to extensor indicis origin
Tendon takes sharp angle after crossing extensor retinaculum to reach distal phalanx of 1st digit
Extends wrist, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, interphalangeal joint of thumb
Extensor Pollicis Brevis
Originates off posterior aspect of radius, interosseus membrane, lateral to EPL
Tendon runs at less of an angle than EPL, attaching to proximal phalanx of 1st digit
Tendons of EPL EPB can be palpated superficially; region between tendons known as anatomical snuff box; landmark for palpation of radial artery as it passes into the hand
Generates extension of wrist, MCP joint, interphalangeal joint
Abductor Pollicis Longus
Broad origin off posterior aspect of radius, ulna, interosseus membrane
Tendon runs laterally alongside extensor pollicis brevis to insert on the base of the 1st metacarpal
Contracts to abduct the 1st digit
Arteries of the Antebrachium
Brachial artery divides in the cubital fossa, just superficial to the biceps tendon, forming the radial and ulnar arteries, respectively
Radial artery supplies blood to lateral portion of the antebrachium, ulnar artery supplies blood to the medial portion
Radial Artery
Courses along the lateral aspect of the forearm, deep to the brachioradialis muscle to reach the wrist
Supplies numerous muscular branches to muscles along the lateral aspect of the arm
Lies superficial just proximal to the wrist, lateral to flexor carpi radialis muscle
Area is ideal for palpation of artery to take pulse count
Artery wraps around base of scaphoid to run along posterior surface of carpal bones
Pulse is also palpable in anatomical snuff box
Radial Recurrent Artery
Branch off the radial artery just distal to the cubital fossa
Curves to run proximally into the arm, just anterior to the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Anastomoses with the radial collateral branch of the brachial artery
Supplies blood to the lateral aspect of the elbow joint
Ulnar Artery
Courses medially between flexors digitorum superficialis and profundus to reach wrist
Supplies numerous muscular branches to muscles along the medial aspect of the arm
Anterior Ulnar Recurrent Artery
First branch off the ulnar artery, just past the division of the brachial artery
Curves to run proximally into the arm, anterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus
Anastomoses with the inferior ulnar collateral branch of the brachial artery
Supplies blood to the anteromedial aspect of the elbow joint
Posterior Ulnar Recurrent Artery
Second branch off the ulnar artery
Curves to run proximally into the arm, posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus
Anastomoses with the superior ulnar collateral branch of the brachial artery
Supplies blood to the posteromedial aspect of the elbow joint
Common Interosseus Artery
Branches off the medial aspect of the ulnar artery, dives deep in the proximal forearm
Posterior branch
Passes between radius and ulna proximal to the interosseus membrane
Gives off recurrent interosseus artery, which travels proximally into brachium, lateral to olecranon process, anastomosing middle collateral artery
Runs along posterior surface of interosseus membrane 2/3rds of the way down to the wrist
Anterior branch
Continues along the anterior surface of the interosseus membrane
Passes between radius and ulna distal to the interosseus membrane to supply the distal posterior region of the antebrachium
Veins of the Antebrachium
Divided into superficial group (draining the cutaneous regions) and deep group (draining the deep structures)
Superficial Veins
Cephalic Vein
Runs along the lateral surface of the antebrachium
Basilic Vein
Runs along the medial surface of the antebrachium
Median Cubital Vein
Variable branch of vein interconnecting the basilic and cephalic veins
Generally runs superomedially, passing superficially in the region of the cubital fossa
A common site for venous blood draws, due to ease of landmarking and access
Deep Veins
Generally follow the same course and named according to the arteries they accompany
Exist as venae commitantes in most instances
Nerves of the Antebrachium
Median Nerve
Enters the forearm by passing between heads of pronator teres

Pronator syndrome – tight pronator muscles from repetitive wrist movement may compress the median nerve at this point, resulting in pain, parasthesia, and/or loss of strength at the wrist; wrist tends to go into ulnar deviation during wrist flexion due to unopposed action of flexor carpi ulnaris
Passes within neurovascular plane between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus
Continues distally lateral to flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, medial to FPL tendon
Enters the wrist through the lateral aspect of the carpal tunnel
With Carpal tunnel syndrome (see above), increase compartmental pressure on median nerve can result in progressive neuropathy; affects muscles innervated by median nerve distal to carpal tunnel
Articular Branches
Branches off the medial nerve that supply the elbow joint
Sensory fibers for touch, pain, proprioception
Muscular Branches
Numerous branches directly off the median nerve supply superficial, intermediate muscles (except flexor carpi ulnaris)
Anterior Interosseus Nerve
Branches off median nerve in proximal region of antebrachium
Runs with anterior interosseus artery along anterior interosseus membrane
Supplies deep compartment of muscles
Terminates with sensory branches at the wrist
Palmar Cutaneous Branch
Small branch off the median nerve just proximal to the carpal tunnel
Cutaneous branch to the hand
Ulnar Nerve
Enters the Forearm posterior to the medial epicondyle
Passes between 2 heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, supplying motor branches to both muscles as it does
Passes through forearm between flexor digitorum profundus and flexor carpi ulnaris supplying motor branches as it does
Emerges superficially to pass into hand between pisiform and hook of the hamate, under band of fibrous connective tissue forming the ulnar (Guyon) canal

Ulnar nerve can become compressed at the wrist from constant pressure (e.g. prolonged pressure from handlebars of bike); results in tingling along cutaneous branches to hand (similar to “funny bone” parasthesia); prolonged compression may result in hand weakness in time
Radial Nerve
Enters the antebrachium by passing anterior to lateral epicondyle, lying between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus muscles, supplying them with muscular branches
Shortly splits into 2 distinct branches
Superficial Branch
Sensory branch continues between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus muscles, eventually emerging cutaneously in the dorsolateral region of the hand
Receives cutaneous sensory information from dorsolateral surface of hand
Deep Branch
Motor branch runs posteriorly around neck of radius to pierce supinator muscle

Supinator syndrome – tight supinator muscle can compress the deep branch of the radial nerve, resulting in weakness to the extensor muscles; results in “drop-wrist” with no effect on elbow extension; often presents as weakness in hand grasping, due to loss of “power grip” position; not associated with pain/parasthesia (no sensory function)
Supplies branches to muscles of the posterior compartment of the arm
Deepest portion commonly referred to as posterior interosseus nerve (synonymous term)
Cutaneous Nerves
Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Continuation of musculcutaneous nerve
Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Branches from the medial cord of the brachial plexus
Posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Branches from the radial nerve in the forearm
