paragraphs.text: The Lower Limb
Images – Netter, plates 471-473
Overview
Extension of the lower trunk
Accept weight directed inferolateral from axis, upper appendices, redistributes inferomedial towards the ground
Result of architecture of innominate (hip bones) distributing weight from sacrum femur, angle of inclination of the neck of the femur
Weight is redistributed from lateral to medial at the neck of the femur

Sight of great bone strain; common site for fractures, particularly in elderly individuals with osteoporosis with sudden hard impact (e.g. missing a step on the stairs); commonly called a broken hip, though it is distal to the hip joint; often impacted, due to orientation of bones, pull of muscles
Functions
Support body weight during standing
Locomotion – movement of body through ground contact force distribution
Balance – adjustments in muscle contraction, joint position maintain center of gravity over base of support
Subcutaneous Structures within the Lower Limb
Fascia Lata
Tough, fiberous fascia that envelops the thigh
Acts like a surgical stocking, compressing deep tissues and preventing pooling of blood
Projects deep to femur, forming 3 septa that divide thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments
Thickest on its lateral side, where it forms the iliotibial band
Aponeurosis that serves as attachment for 2 muscles (gluteus maximus and tensor fascia lata)
Inserts on the lateral aspect of the tibia
Saphenous opening – oval region found superomedially where fascia lata thins into membranous cribriform fascia
Permits communication of cutaneous structures (lymphatics, great saphenous vein) with deep structures
Crural Fascia
Deep fascia of the leg that is continuous with fascia lata superiorly
Invaginations form anterior and posterior intermuscular septa, that help divide the leg into anterior, lateral and posterior compartments
Transverse intermuscular septum further divides the posterior compartment into superficial, deep groups
Thickest over the anterior compartment, where underlying muscle attaches to it
Forms extensor retinacula at the ankle joint
Cutaneous Venous Drainage
Numerous venous tributaries, most of which are unnamed
Great Saphenous Vein
Longest continuous vein in the body

Starts at the dorsomedial surface of the foot, ascends anterior to the ankle on its medial side, crosses posterior to the knee, curves anterior in the medial thigh to merge with the femoral vein through the saphenous opening
Represents the main tributary of venous return in the superficial leg, receives numerous smaller tributaries along its path
Portions of the great saphenous are often removed to serve as bypass vessels in coronary artery bypass graft surgery; type of autograft
Small Saphenous Vein
Major tributary on the posterolateral surface of the leg
Ascends posterior to the ankle on its lateral side and pierces the deep fascia along the posterior surface of the knee (popliteal fossa)to drain into the deep venous network
Cutaneous Lymphatic Drainage
Lymph vessels typically accompany superficial veins towards the saphenous opening
Drain into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes surrounding the saphenous opening
Superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain through saphenous opening to communicate with deep lymphatic nodes/vessels within the pelvis, upper thigh
Lymph vessels accompanying small saphenous vein drain with it through the popliteal fossa and the deep lymphatics located there
Cutaneous Nerves
Extensive branching, typically arising from a small set of distinct main branches
Anterior nerves of the thigh
Branches off the femoral nerve supplying the anterior thigh
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Direct branch from the lumbar plexus supplying the lateral thigh
Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Direct branch from the sacral plexus supplying the posterior thigh
Superior/inferior clunial nerves
Branches of varying origin supplying the gluteal region
Superficial fibular nerve
Braches off the common fibular nerve to supply the anterior leg, dorsum of foot
Saphenous nerve
Distinct branch off femoral nerve
Emerges proximal with the knee to run with the saphenous vein
Supplies the medial aspect of the leg
Sural nerve
Supplies the lateral/posterior aspect of the leg
Typically a fusion of lateral and medial sural cutaneous nerves, both of which branch from the sciatic nerve
Anterior and Medial Thigh
Images – Netter, plates 480-481, 488-489
Overview
Thigh is organized into 3 principal compartments
Anterior
Located at the front of the femur
Muscular compartment involved in hip flexion, knee extension
Innervated by femoral nerve
Medial
Located medial to the femur
Muscular compartment involved in hip adduction
Innervated by obturator nerve
Posterior
Located beind the femur
Muscular compartment involved in hip extension, knee flexion
Innervated by sciatic nerve
(Discussed in a later set of notes)
Main Neurovascular bundle supplying vasculature, innervation to the lower limb travels between anterior, medial compartment
Os Coxae: the Pelvic Bone
Principle framework for the pelvis
Articulates with the sacrum proximally and femur distally
Composed of 3 separate bones joined through hyaline cartilage
Fusion begins in late adolescence; complete by 25 years of age
Ileum
Largest of the pelvic bones; lies superiorly
Inferior body projects superiorly into broad thin ala (wings)
Iliac crest forms superior margin of the ala
Terminates anteriorly into anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) – muscle attachment
Terminates posteriorly into posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) – muscle attachment
Auricular surface – ear shaped medial surface that articulates with sacrum
Ischium
Posteroinferior bone of the pelvis
Ischial spine – posterior projection for ligamentous attachment
Landmark for greater sciatic notch superiorly, lesser sciatic notch inferiorly
Ischial ramus projects anteromedially to fuse with inferior pubic ramus
Forms lower border of obturator foramen
Ischial tuberosity found posteroinferiorly
Supports weight in sitting position
Attachment of hamstring muscles
Pubis
Anteroinferior bone of the pelvis
Medial bodies articulate at midline through symphysis pubis
Superior and inferior rami project laterally, forming superior/inferior margin of obturator foramen
Femur: the Bone of the Thigh
Longest bone in the body
Accepts weight from os coxae, redirects it medially
Articulates with os coxae through femoral head
Small indentation in head called fovea centralis – attachment for round ligament, nutrient artery
Head injuries may sever round ligament, disrupt artery, resulting in loss of blood flow to the head of the femur; bone tissue degenerates with time, causing avascular necrosis and joint degeneration
Neck projects inferolaterally from head
Angle of inclination – angle that neck makes with shaft as weight is redistributed medially
Greater, lesser trocanters serve as sites for muscle attachment
Shaft is directed medially towards knee
Partially bowed (concave medially) to absorb impact forces
Ricketts – bone demineralization due to vitamin D deficiency (usually due to lack of sun exposure); results in excessive bowing of legs in response to stress of weight bearing
Rough posterior surface, location of gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera
Attachment of gluteus maximus, quadriceps femoris, respectively
Shaft terminates in medial, lateral condyles for articulation with the knee
Medial, lateral epicondyles sites for attachment of the collateral ligaments
Hip Joint
Synovial ball-and-socket joint between acetabulum of os coxae and head of femur
Femoral head articulates with lunate surface within superior margin of acetabulum
Surface area of acetabulum increased by presence of acetabular labrum; continuous with transverse acetabular ligament
Covers more than half of femoral head at a given position
Joint capsule anchored to acetabulum external to labrum, projects anteriorly in spiral fashion to attach to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly
Strong resistance to hyperextension
Lack of posterior anchor allows synovial membrane to protrude posteriorly, forming bursa to cushion overlying muscle
3 thickenings form intercapsular ligaments
Iliofemoral ligament
Runs from AIIS, acetabular rim to intertochanteric line
Extremely strong
Resists hyperextension of the hip joint through corkscrew mechanism
Ischiofemoral ligament
Runs from posterior acetabular rim
Relatively weak
Resists hyperextension
Pubofemoral ligament
Originates inferiorly off obturator crest of pubic bone
Prevents hyperabduction of joint (e.g. during splits)
Synovial membrane anchors to periphery of articular surface of femoral head, with numerous folds for increased mobility
Surrounds the functionally weak ligamentum capitis femoris (ligament to the head of the femur)
Runs from acetabular notch to fovea capitis on the head of the femur
Conducts the artery to the head of the femur for vascular supply
Disruption of this artery may lead to avascular necrosis, degeneration of the femoral head
Multi-axial joint
Permits flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, circumduction, and rotation
Ligaments limit extension through corkscrew mechanism
Flexion only limited through soft tissue apposition (thigh against abdomen)
NB: lateral rotators stronger than medial rotators; provide greater stabilization than ligaments posteriorly
Muscles of the Anterior Compartment
Quadriceps Femoris
Largest muscle of the anterior compartment
Principle extensor of the knee
Consists of 4 identifiable heads that converge on the quadriceps tendon to attach to the patella and on to the tibial tuberosity
Rectus femoris
Originates off the anterior inferior iliac spine of the os coxae
Descends through the thigh and is enveloped by the other 3 quadriceps muscles
Think: a hotdog in a bun
Only quadriceps belly to cross the hip
Contributes to hip flexion in addition to knee extension
Vastus lateralis
Originates off gluteal tuberosity, lateral lip of linea aspera
Curves laterally to attach to the patella
Vastus medialis
Originates off medial lip of linea aspera
Curves medially to attach to the patella
Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) – specific reference to most inferior part of vastus medialis
Line of pull of quadriceps tends to pull patella laterally; countered by VMO fibers; weak VMO associated with poor patellar tracking, lateral dislocation
Vastus Intermedius
Originates off anterior surface of femur
Lies deep to the rectus femoris belly
Sartorius
a.k.a. the “taylor” muscle
longest continuous muscle in the body
Originates off the Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS), curves medially along the vastus medialis to cross posterior to the knee joint
Inserts on the anteromedial aspect of the tibia at the pes anserinus (goose’s foot)
The “cross-legged” muscle
Flexes, abducts, laterally rotates the hip
Flexes the knee
Iliopsoas
Combination of 2-3 muscles originating from the pelvis
Psoas major – off the lumbar vertebrae
Psoas minor (if present) – off the lumbar vertebrae
Iliacus – off the anterior surface of the ilium
Insert through common tendon to lesser trochanter
Principle flexor of the thigh
Pectineus
“Hybrid” of anterior, medial compartment muscles
Dual innervation from both compartments (femora and obturator n.s)
Functions overlap those of muscles in both compartments
Originates off superior ramus of pubis
Inserts on pectineal line of femur, just distal to lesser trochanter
Adducts, flexes, medially rotates hip
Muscles of the Medial Compartment
All muscles innervated by obturator nerve
All muscles generate hip adduction
Obturator Externus
Most superior of the medial compartment
Originates of the obturator membrane
Inserts to the trochanteric fossa just medial to the greater trochanter
Lateral rotator, stabilizer of hip joint
Adductor Longus
Originates of pubic bone close to symphysis pubis
Inserts on middle third of linea aspera
Adductor Brevis
Originates off the pubic bone just inferior to the adductor longus muscle
Runs posteriorly to both pectineus and adductor longus to attach to proximal portion of linea aspera
Adductor Magnus
Broadest of the adductor muscles
“Hybrid” muscle with 2 distinct regions
Adductor portion – innervation/action of medial compartment muscle
Hamstring portion – innervation/action of posterior compartment muscle
Originates off inferior rami of ischium/pubic bones, just anterior to hamstring origin
Insertion
Adductor portion – along full length of linea aspera
Hamstring portion – adductor tubercle of femur
Arch between portions at attachment to femur creates space known as adductor hiatus
Allows passage of vessels between anterior, posterior compartments of thigh, leg
Gracilis
Originates of pubic bone inferior to adductor brevis muscle
Runs posterior to knee to insert with sartorius on pes anserinus
Also assists with knee flexion, in addition to hip adduction
The Femoral Triangle
Triangular landmark with anatomical/clinical importance
Borders
Superior – inguinal canal
Subinguinal canal – space between inguinal ligament, floor of triangle that permits communication between anterior compartment of leg and pelvis
Medial – adductor longus m.
Lateral – Sartorius m.
Apex found inferiorly, where Sartorius crosses adductor longus
Floor formed by pectineus, iliopsoas muscles
Covered by facia lata and cruciform fascia (over saphenous opening)
Contents
Important transit of neurovascular structures to and from lower limb
Vascular structures embedded in femoral sheath, a distinct fascial tube about 3-4 cm in length
Blends with superficial connective tissue of vessels distally
Think: elastic band on sweatshirt sleeve
Permits gliding of vascular structures during flexion/extension of the hip
Femoral Nerve
Most lateral structure in the triangle
Found on anterior surface of psoas major, embedded in its fascia
Already extensively divided into cutaneous, muscular branches
Terminal branch called the saphenous nerve, travels through abductor canal with femoral vessels, emerging
Femoral Artery
Most lateral structure within the femoral sheath
Found at midway point of subinguinal canal
Primary artery supply of the lower limb

Injury to the proximal region of the femoral artery can result in extensive blood loss, death within minutes; artery can be compressed by landmarking mid-region of femoral triangle cutaneously and applying pressure
Projects down the adductor canal with saphenous nerve
Passes through the adductor hiatus to access the popliteal fossa, where it becomes the tibial artery
Profunda Femoris Artery
The deep artery of the thigh
Primary supply to the anterior compartment
Gives off medial and lateral femoral circumflex branches to supply the femoral head and neck
Lateral femoral circumflex gives off 2 additional branches
Transverse branch particularly important in supplying blood to the head of the femur
Descending branch supplies lateral part of anterior compartment, knee
Gives off several perforating branches further down
Pierce adductor muscles to access the posterior compartment
Ensures continued blood flow in sitting position
Femoral Vein
Lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle
Projects with femoral artery to the adductor hiatus, where it becomes the popliteal vein
Drains perforating branches, great saphenous vein before passing under subinguinal canal
Femora Canal
Empty space in femoral sheath found medial to the femoral vein
Permits expansion of artery during systole
Deep Lymphatic vessels/nodes
Found in most medial region of femoral sheath
Drain lymph from the deep structures in the lower limb, passing lymph to deep nodes within the pelvis
Occasionally drains lymph from superficial lymphatics
Adductor (Subsartorial) Canal
Muscular compartment distal to the apex of the femoral triangle
Borders
Anterolateral – vastus medialis
Posterior – adductors longus and magnus
Covered by Sartorius muscle
Allows passage of femoral vessels to adductor hiatus, saphenous nerve to leg, motor branch to VMO
Vessels covered inferiorly by tough subsartorial fascia
Obturator Canal
Obturator foramen covered by obturator membrane
Sight for muscle attachment of obturator externus/internus muscles
Obturator canal results from incomplete covering of the foramen
Typically found at the medial margins of the membrane
Permits access of obturator artery, nerve to the medial compartment of the thigh

title: The Lower Limb

paragraphs.text: The Hand
Readings – Netter’s Clinical Anatomy, pgs. 377 - 392
Overview
Distal-most region of the upper appendage
Intricate dexterity – precision contractions and opposable digit allow grasping, manipulation with great deal of control
Opposition due to 900 rotation of 1st digit
Palmar region found anteriorly, dorsal region found posteriorly
Bones of the hand
Divided into 3 regions
Carpal bones
The bones of the wrist
Articulate with radius, ulna through wrist joint proximally, metacarpals distally
8 bones arranged in 2 rows of 4
Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrium, pisiform
Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
Interconnected through flat articulating surfaces bound by dense ligaments
Permits small degree of gliding
Subtle, but necessary for normal hand function

Joints are often tight, restrictive following cast removal for fractured forearm, wrist; limits hand movements (grasping, pulp-to-pulp opposition); part of rehabilitative therapy involves carpal joint mobilization to improve function
Metacarpal Bones
Associated with the distal palm
Composed of 5 small long bones
Base found proximally, articulating with carpal bones
Digit 1 – saddle joint
Head found distally, articulating with phalanges
Makes up “knuckles” of the fist
Metacarpal fractures common, resulting from improper punches, punching hard surfaces; 3rd metacarpal particularly vulnerable, due to its length
Phalanges
Associated with the fingers
Series of very small long bones
2 in digit 1 (proximal and distal), 3 in digits 2 through 5 (proximal, middle, and distal)
Articulate with metacarpals through condyloid joints
Permits flexion, extension, abduction, adduction
Interarticulations through hinge joints
Permits flexion, extension only
Fascia and Compartments
Hand enveloped in single layer of superficial fascia continuous with the fascia of the forearm
Specialized in various regions, depending on function
Fascia helps to divide hand into 5 distinct compartments; each compartment houses different set of muscles
NB: all 5 compartments associated with palmar surface; no dorsal compartments, intrinsic muscles
Palmar Fascia
Covers the palmer surface
Thickest in midregion of palm, where it forms palmar aponeurosis
Dense regular connective tissue projecting distally towards digits
Due in part to insertion of plamaris longus tendon
Projects into palmar surface of digits, forming fibrous digital sheaths that envelop flexor tendons
Projects deep in palmar surface of hand dividing palm into separate compartments
Dupuytren Contracture – fibrosis/shortening of medial aspect of palmer aponeurosis, resulting in contracture of 4th and 5th digits
Fibers oriented transversely just distal to the wrist
Superficial transverse fibers commonly called the palmar carpal ligament, but officially unnamed
Very thin – similar and continuous with extensor retinaculum on posterior side
Holds all flexor tendons in place, preventing bowstringing
Deeper, thicker transverse fibers run from  scaphoid/trapezium to pisiform/hook of hamate, forming the flexor retinaculum, (transverse carpal ligament)
Forms the roof of the carpal tunnel
Separates wrist/digital flexors
Wrist flexors (flexor carpi) found superficial to transverse ligament
Digital flexors (flexor digitorum) found deep to transverse ligament
Thins out drastically on either side of flexor retinaculum, where it envelops thenar and hypothenar eminences as loose aerolear connective tissue
Palmaris brevis – small, thin muscle that runs transversely in palmar fascia over hypothenar eminence
Anchors dermis over hypothenar eminence to palmar aponeurosis
Contracts to wrinkle skin, deepen palmar furrow
Soft protection for ulnar artery/nerve
Dorsal Fascia
Much thinner than palmar fascia
Thickest just distal to the wrist, where it forms the extensor retinaculum
Central Compartment
Located deep to palmar aponeurosis
Medial/lateral borders formed by deep fascial projections off palmar aponeurosis
Houses digital flexor tendons
Midpalmar space – potential space between central, interosseous compartment
Assists with tendon gliding
Thenar Compartment
Located lateral to central compartment
Contains thenar muscles, forming fleshy tissue at base of thumb
Thenar space – potential space between thenar, adductor compartments
Allows gliding between compartments
Hypothenar Compartment
Located medial to central compartment
Contains hypothenar muscles, forming fleshy tissue at base of small finger
Interosseus Compartment
Located between metacarpals
Contains dorsal, palmar interossei muscles
NB: despite name, dorsal interossei still considered part of palmar surface
Adductor Compartment
Intermediate to thenar/interosseus compartments
Contains adductor pollicis muscle
Muscles of the Hand
Thenar Muscles
Located at base of thumb (pollicis) in thenar compartment
Common origin off flexor retinaculum, lateral carpal bones (scaphoid, trapezium)
Involved with precision movement of the thumb
Particularly important for opposition
Loss of function (e.g. deinnervation) results in muscle atrophy, loss of opposition; antagonistic muscles pull thumb into extension (ape-hand deformity)
Flexor Pollicis Brevis
Superficial medial portion of the thenar eminence
Two headed muscle (superficial and deep) separated by FPL tendon
Inserts on proximal phalanx
Assists FPL with metacarpophalangeal flexion
Abductor Pollicis Brevis
Superficial lateral portion of the thenar eminence
Inserts on proximal phalanx
Assists APL with metacarpophalangeal abduction
Opponens Pollicis
Deep portion of the thenar eminence
Inserts on 1st metacarpal
Contracts to generate complex movement of thumb opposition (flexion, internal rotation of 1st carpometacarpal joint drawing pulp of thumb towards other fingers)
Hypothenar Eminence
Located at base of little finger (digiti minimi) in hypothenar compartment
Common origin off flexor retinaculum and carpal bones (pisiform, hook of hamate)
Involved with precise movement of little finger
Flexor Digiti Minimi Brevis
Lies superficial and lateral (inside border) in the hypothenar eminence
Inserts on outside of proximal phalanx
Flexor of MCP joint
NB: flexor digiti minimi longus represents rare anatomical variant: not normally present in humans nor discussed in anatomical texts
Abductor Digiti Minimi
Found superficial and medial (outside border) of hypothenar eminence
Inserts on outside of proximal phalanx
Abductor of MCP joint
Opponens DigitiMinimi
Deep portion of the thenar eminence
Inserts on 5th metacarpal
Generates opposition in little finger (flexion, internal rotation of 5th carpometacarpal joint)
Adductor Pollicis
Only muscle of the adductor compartment
Belly divides into 2 heads
Oblique head – originates off base of 2nd, 3rd metacarpal
Transverse head – originates off shaft of 3rd metacarpal
Inserts on proximal phalanx of thumb
Adducts thumb, contributes to grip strength
Lumbricals
Four small cylindrical muscles
NB: lumbrical – earthworm
Originate off FDP tendon
Two lateral lumbricals (1 and 2) have single origin off lateral border of tendons to 2nd and 3rd digit
Two medial lumbricals (3 and 4) bipennate, originating off medial and lateral borders of adjacent tendons to digits 3 through 5
Tendon cross anterior to MCP joints on their lateral sides, project posteriorly to insert on lateral bands of extensor hood
Unique insertion results in flexion of MCP joint, extension of interphalangeal joints

Commonly paralyzed following nerve damage to brachial plexus (Klumpke’s palsy), medial nerve, or ulnar nerve; loss of intrinsic function (MCP flexion, IP extension) results in unopposed pull of antagonistic muscles leading to claw finger deformity (MCP extension, IP flexion); variability in specific lumbrical muscles paralyzed, depending on site of nerve damage (due to innervation by different nerves) results in different deformity presentations
Interossei Muscles
Found within the interosseus compartment
Tendons cross anterior to MCP joints to attach to base of proximal phalanges, expansion of extensor hood
Similar course to lumbrical muscles; also produce MCP flexion, IP extension
Interossei commonly paralyzed along with lumbricals (similar innervation pattern), further contributing to claw finger/hand deformity
Palmar Interossei
Three unipennate muscles originating off sides of 2nd, 4th, and 5th metacarpal bones
Come off side closest to midline
2nd – medial
4th and 5th – lateral
Insert on side of proximal phalange closest to midline
Contract to pull digits 2, 4, 5 closer to digit 3 (adduction)
Think: 3 PAD
Dorsal Interossei
Four bipennate muscles originating off both sides of adjacent metacarpals
Tendons insert on base of proximal phalange furthest away from midline
Arrangement permits abduction during contraction
Think: 4 DAB
Long Tendons of the Hand
Flexor Digitorum Tendons
Digital flexor tendons (from FDS and FDP) enter hand through carpal tunnel encased in common flexor sheath (ulnar bursa)
Bursal membrane separates each row of tendons, preventing friction
Think: water-filled garbage bag
In central compartment, tendons of FDS, FDP disperse to digits 2 through 5
As tendons approach MCP joint, become encased in digital synovial sheaths similar to common flexor tendon sheaths that continues to distal insertion point

Synovial sheath of 5th digit continuous with common flexor sheath; while tenosynovitis (synovial sheath infections from deep lacerations) of digits 2 through 4 remain localized, synovial sheath infection in digit 5 can spread to central compartment, carpal tunnel
Tendons and sheaths covered by fibrous sheath anteriorly that forms osseofibrous tunnel
Prevents bowstringing of tendons

Quervain tenovaginitis stenosans – fibrous thickening of sheaths and stenosis of osseofibrous tunnel due to excessive friction in tendons; may result in tendons getting “caught” in tunnel, producing painful snapping on flexion/extension (trigger finger)
Past MCP joint, FDS tendons bifurcate, attach bilaterally to base of middle phalanges
Tendons of FDP continue along midline of digit, emerging from beneath FDS at bifurcation point, to insert on base of distal phalanges
Flexor Pollicis Longus Tendon
Enters hand through carpal tunnel lateral to digital flexor tendons
Curves laterally to enter thenar compartment and continues on to base of distal phalanx of 1st digit
Constitutes a single tendon wrapped in a continuous tendonous sheath from carpal tunnel to distal insertion (radial bursa)
Extensor Digitorum Tendons
Major component of dorsum of hand
Enter hand deep to extensor retinaculum to continue to digits 2 through 5
At the MCP joint, the tendon splits, broadens into aponeurosis called extensor expansion (dorsal hood)
Central (median) bands continues along midline of digit to insert at base of middle phalanges
Partial bifurcation generates lateral bands, which diverge along proximal phalanges, converge and insert upon distal phalanges
Receive lumbrical, interossei attachment
Vasculature of the Hand
Arterial supply from extensive anastomoses of radial, ulnar arteries
Poses difficulties with severe lacerations to arteries of the hand; often the brachial artery is compressed to prevent excessive bleeding during surgical repair
Superficial Palmar Arch
Superficial arterial arcade supplied by superficial branches of the ulnar artery medially and the radially artery laterally
Ulnar > radial
Gives off 3 common palmar branches between digits 2 through 5
Each branch splits at MCP joint to form proper digital branches
Raynaud syndrome – idiopathic ischemia of digital arteries, typically in response to cold, stress, resulting in pain and/or parasthesia
Course along medial/lateral sides of adjacent digits
Gives off single proper digital branch to medial side of 5th digit
Deep Palmer Arch
Deep arterial arcade supplied by deep branches of the ulnar artery medially and the radially artery laterally
Ulnar < radial
Gives off 3 palmar metacarpal branches
Anastamose with common palmer branches anteriorly
Gives off radialis indicis artery
Supplies blood to lateral aspect of 2nd digit
Gives off Princeps pollicis artery
Splits to supply digital branches to the thumb
Nerves of the Hand
Median Nerve
Enters hand through carpal tunnel

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome – results from increased compartmental pressure in the carpal tunnel; caused by inflammation of tendons, ulnar/radial bursa or blunt force trauma; pressure causes neural degeneration of median nerve, resulting in loss of function
Gives off recurrent branch to thenar eminence; innervation of thenar muscles (except deep head of FPB)
Injury to any part of the median nerve results in loss of function of thenar eminence, progressing to ape-hand deformity without recovery
Branches into common/proper digital nerves between digits 1 through 4.
Supply motor branches to lumbricals 1 and 2
Injury to any part of the median nerve results in loss of function of lumbricals supplying digits 2 and 3, progression to digital claw deformity for these 2 digits, exclusively (“median nerve claw”)
When asked to make fist, loss of function results in incomplete flexion of digits 2 and 3 (the “Hand of Benediction” sign)
Proper digital nerves receive cutaneous innervation from digits 1 through 3, lateral half of digit 4
Ulnar Nerve
Enters hand through ulnar canal between pisiform and hook of hamate, medial to ulnar artery
Provides branches to hypothenar eminence
Deep branch courses with deep palmer arch
Supplies motor branches to interossei, adductor pollicis, deep head of FPB
Superficial branch splits to provide common digital branch between digits 4 and 5, proper digital branch to digit 5
Gives off motor branches to 3rd and 4th lumbricals
Proper digital branches receive cutaneous innervation from digit 5, medial half of digit 4

Ulnar nerve supplies majority of muscles in the hand; injury to the ulnar nerve proximal to the hand would result in extensive loss of hand function, progressing to “ulnar nerve claw” deformity; more pronounced claw deformity for digits 4 and 5 (loss of lumbricals, interossei) and less pronounced claw deformity for digits 2 and 3 (loss of interossei, only);
Radial Nerve
Superficial branch enters the hand superficial to the palmar fascia
Receives cutaneous innervation to base of thumb, back of hand

paragraphs.text: The Leg
Overview
Region between thigh and foot
Continuous proximally with the thigh at the knee joint
Continuous distally with the foot at the ankle joint
Tibia, fibula, interosseus membrane, and deep projections of the crural fascia (intermuscular septa) divide the leg into 4 separate compartments
Anterior compartment
Houses the dorsiflexors (ankle extensors), digital extensors
Vascular supply by anterior tibial a.
Innervated by the deep fibular nerve
Lateral compartment
Houses the everters of the ankle
Vascular supply by fibular a.
Innervated by the superficial fibular nerve
Superficial posterior compartment
Houses the plantar flexors (ankle flexors)
Vascular supply by posterior tibial a., fibular a.
Innervated by tibial n.
Deep posterior compartment
Houses both plantar flexors and digital flexors
Vascular supply by posterior tibial a., fibular a.
Innervated by tibial n.
Vascular Supply
Lower leg almost entirely supplied by popliteal artery
Continuation of femoral artery past adductor hiatus
Runs posterior to knee joint (protection)
Gives of  superior (medial & lateral) and inferior (medial & lateral) genicular branches that anastamose around knee
Just distal to proximal tibiofibular joint, divides into…
Anterior tibial artery
Passes between tibia, fibula, courses along anterior surface of interosseus membrane
Supplies blood to anterior compartment
Continues distal to ankle as dorsalis pedis
Runs between tendons of EDL and EHL (palpable pulse) to supply dorsal arch
Posterior tibial artery
Continues medially in deep posterior compartment behind tibia, supplying posterior compartments
Gives off fibular artery
Runs laterally in deep posterior compartment, supplying posterior, lateral compartments
Posterior tibial artery passes posterior to medial malleolus to enter plantar surface of foot, branching into medial and lateral plantar arteries
Innervation
Most sensory, all motor innervation from sciatic nerve
Travels through posterior compartment of thigh
Made up of 2 distinct nerves bundled together, functionally separate throughout path
At variable level sciatic divides into…
Tibial nerve
Runs posterior to knee to course through septum separating superficial, deep posterior compartments
Supplies both posterior compartment
Passes posterior to medial malleolus to enter plantar surface of foot, branching into medal and lateral plantar nerves
Supplies intrinsic muscles of plantar surface of foot
Common fibular nerve
Courses superficially around head of fibula
Susceptible to injury due to superficial location; nerve lesion would result in loss of dorsiflexion, eversion
Divides into…
Superficial fibular nerve
Supplies the lateral compartment of the leg
Deep fibular nerve
Supplies the anterior compartment of the leg
Continues into dorsum of foot to supply intrinsic dorsal muscles
Joints of the Foot
The Ankle Joint
Synovial hinge-type joint
Articulation between tibia/fibula and talus
Mortois shape
Anterior Compartment of the Leg
Readings – Moore, pgs. 587-595
Images – Netter, plates 507-510
Overview
One of 4 recognized compartments of the leg
Lateral to tibia
Anterior to fibula, interosseus membrane
Divides anterior from deep posterior compartment
Medial to anterior intermuscular septum
Divides anterior from lateral compartment
Superficial muscles of compartment partially attached to overlying thickening of crural fascia for stronger anchoring
Anterior Compartment Syndrome
Thickness of investing fascia, combined with relatively confined space, prevents any large degree of expansion
Chronic inflammation or progressive enlargement of muscles in compartment can lead to gradual increase in compartmental pressure
Results in neuropathy, muscle weakness, inability to dorsiflex against gravity (drop foot)
Characteristic change in gait to compensate
Acute swelling from trauma may compromise circulation to lower leg
Can lead to tissue necrosis, gangrene, amputation if left untreated
Fascial release – condition sometimes treated with incision through overlying crural fascia, allowing expansion of compartment and decrease of pressure
Extensor retinaculum
Superior – straight band found proximal to ankle joint
Inferior – Y-band found inferior to ankle joint
Muscles
All muscles assist with dorsiflexion
All muscles innervated by deep fibular nerve
Tibialis Anterior
Lies superficial, medial in compartment
Originates from top half of lateral surface of tibia, medial margin of interosseus membrane
Long tendon runs medial and inferior to cross anterior to ankle joint under retinacula
Tendon projects anteriorly away from joint, giving TA significant mechanical advantage
Inserts on inferior surface of medial cuneiform, base of 1st metatarsal
Ankle inverter in addition to dorsiflexor
Extensor Digitorum Longus
Lies superficial, lateral in compartment
Originates off medial surface of fibula, part of lateral margin of interosseus membrane proximally
Generates four tendons encased in common synovial sheath that pass under retinacula directly anterior to ankle joint
Insert on dorsal surface of phalanges
Form extensor hood identical to ED of antebrachium, but less developed
Digital extensor in addition to dorsiflexor
Fibularis Tertius Muscle
Vestigial muscle (not always present)
Originates off medial surface of fibula, just distal to EDL
Fibers blend with EDL, crosses ankle in same synovial sheath
Tendon projects laterally to insert on dorsal surface of 5th metatarsal
Weak dorsiflexor, evertor of ankle
Potential role in proprioception – stretch reflex during sudden inversion (ankle rolling) to trigger evertors to protect ligaments
NB: despite name, not to be confused for a lateral compartment muscle
Extensor Hallucis Longus
Lies deep, central in compartment
Originates off medial surface of fibula, lateral margin of interosseus membrane distal and medial to EDL
Tendon protrudes between TA, EDL as it crosses ankle to insert on distal phalanx of great toe
Extensor of 1st digit
Lateral Compartment of the Leg
Readings – Moore, pgs. 595-596
Images – Netter, plates 507-510
Overview
One of 4 recognized compartments of the leg
Lateral to fibula, anterior intermuscular septum
Divides lateral from anterior compartment
Anterior to posterior intermuscular septum
Divides lateral from posterior compartments
Ends inferiorly at the superior  fibular retinaculum
Muscles
Evertors, plantar flexors of the ankle
Innervated by superficial fibular nerve
Fibularis Longus
Originates off lateral surface of proximal fibular shaft
Tendon runs superficial to fibularis brevis; crosses posterior to lateral malleolus, curves medially to run obliquely in deep plantar compartment of foot
Inserts on lateral margin of medial cuneiform, 1st metatarsal
Fibularis Brevis
Originates off lateral surface of distal fibular shaft
Tendon runs deep to fibularis longus; crosses posterior to lateral malleolus, runs anteriorly to insert on base of 5th metatarsal
Forceful plantar flexion can result in avulsion fractures; tendon of fibularis brevis pulls segment of base of 5th metatarsal bone off
